title: SBI quarterly results: Bank shares decline despite loan growth, better asset quality in Q2 - What it means to investors | Stock Market News
snippet: Shares of State Bank of India (SBI), the country's largest public sector lender, erased their intraday gains in Tuesday's trade on November 3, falling 1.70% to close at ₹970, even as the bank's ...
content:
Shares of State Bank of India (SBI), the country's largest public sector lender, erased their intraday gains in Tuesday's trade on November 3, falling 1.70% to close at ₹970, even as the bank's September-quarter performance came in ahead of Street estimates. The state-owned lender reported a 14.28% year-on-year (YoY) increase in standalone net profit to ₹23,038 crore for the second quarter ended September 30, 2026, supported by strong credit growth and a one-time gain from the sale of shares in its fund management subsidiary earlier in the year. The bank had reported a net profit of ₹20,160 crore in the July-September quarter a year ago. Its net interest income (NII), which is the difference between interest earned on loans and interest paid on deposits, increased 14.69% YoY to ₹49,143 crore during the reporting quarter. SBI's domestic net interest margin (NIM) expanded by 11 basis points from the preceding quarter to 3.11%. SBI's loan book expanded 3.2% over the previous quarter to ₹52.08 lakh crore. Retail, agriculture, and MSME (RAM) advances grew 17.34% YoY, driven by 22.64% growth in agricultural loans, 21.97% in SME advances, and 14.54% in retail personal loans. Corporate advances also increased 16.12% YoY. India's credit growth is gaining momentum as festive-season spending drives consumer borrowing, while companies are also increasing their reliance on bank loans. Banks have raised nearly $133 billion through foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians under a special Reserve Bank of India (RBI) scheme, supporting deposit and credit growth. However, the higher cost of attracting these deposits has put pressure on banks' margins. Meanwhile, SBI's total deposits increased 12.27% YoY, with current account and savings account (CASA) deposits growing 8.13%. The CASA ratio stood at 38.32% as of September 30, 2026, while retail term deposits grew 16.74% YoY. SBI's operating profit grew 7.28% YoY to ₹34,226 crore in Q2 FY27. The bank's return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE) stood at 1.14% and 18.68%, respectively, in the first half of FY27. On asset quality, the bank's gross non-performing asset (NPA) ratio dropped by 34 basis points (bps) YoY to 1.39%, while the net NPA ratio declined by 6 bps to 0.36%. The provision coverage ratio (PCR) stood at 74.43%, rising to 91.83% when accounts under collection were included. Meanwhile, the slippage ratio improved by 4 bps YoY to 0.41% in Q2 FY27, while the credit cost declined by 17 bps YoY to 0.22%. The lender reported an exceptional gain of ₹7,290 crore from the sale of its stake in SBI Funds Management Ltd. State Bank of India and France's Amundi SA offered up to 203.71 million shares in the country's largest fund house by assets. The bank also divested a 0.65% stake in the National Stock Exchange (NSE) during its IPO. However, SBI said the profit from the sale was credited to capital reserves without being routed through the profit and loss account. title: Microsoft Q1 FY2027 Earnings Preview: Azure Must Hit 45%, and Capex Must Start Paying Off
snippet: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) reports fiscal Q1 2027 results after the close, expected on October 28. Management set a high bar in July: revenue of $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, Azure growth of about 45% in constant currency, and roughly $50 billion of ...
content:
Microsoft Q1 FY2027 Earnings Preview: Azure Must Hit 45%, and Capex Must Start Paying Off
Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) reports fiscal Q1 2027 results after the close, expected on October 28. Management set a high bar in July: revenue of $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, Azure growth of about 45% in constant currency, and roughly $50 billion of quarterly capital spending. Azure has to meet that guide, but the bigger questions are cash flow and quality. Q4 free cash flow fell to $19.6 billion as capex hit $41 billion. Commercial bookings grew 18% excluding OpenAI but only 11% including it. One-time items also flattered the last quarter. The setup favors a stock that is priced for execution, with little room for an Azure miss.
Microsoft enters this report from a position of strength. Its July results added roughly $450 billion in market value in one session, the largest single-day gain in the company’s history, after Azure growth accelerated to 43% and capex guidance came in below Wall Street’s fears. Since then, investors have shifted from asking whether AI demand exists to asking whether the spending required to serve it will translate into cash.
What did Microsoft guide for fiscal Q1 2027?
Microsoft’s guidance is the benchmark that matters most. For the September quarter, management guided revenue to $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, up 16% at the midpoint, and Azure growth of about 45% in constant currency, well above the 41.4% StreetAccount consensus at the time. Morningstar calculated an implied operating margin of 48.5% and EPS of $4.70 at the midpoints, with capex guided to about $50 billion.
Other details shape the read. Microsoft expects the Microsoft Cloud gross margin to stay roughly stable from 65% in the prior quarter. Intelligent Cloud revenue is guided to grow 33% to 34%. CFO Amy Hood said Azure growth should continue to accelerate through the first half of fiscal 2027, while warning that growth rates can vary quarter to quarter with capacity timing and contract mix.
An Azure print below about 45% would be the clearest disappointment. A print above it, combined with no further capex increase, is the bull scenario.
How strong was Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 finish?
Very strong on the headline numbers, somewhat less so beneath them. Q4 revenue reached $90.0 billion, up 18% (17% in constant currency), beating the high end of guidance at $87.8 billion, and adjusted EPS was $4.74. For fiscal 2026, revenue rose 18% to $331.8 billion, and operating income climbed 21% to more than $155 billion.
Azure carried the quarter. Azure and other cloud services grew 43%, ahead of the 39% to 40% guide, and full-year Azure revenue topped $100 billion for the first time, up 41%. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $59.3 billion in Q4 and $214.4 billion for the year. Intelligent Cloud grew 32% to $39.3 billion, while Productivity and Business Processes rose 14% to $37.8 billion.
Two details temper the headline. First, Microsoft said several one-time items added $0.27 per share relative to its own guidance, including a $3.2 billion gain on its Anthropic investment, partly offset by severance costs and Xbox impairment charges. Second, gross margin fell year over year to 67% as AI infrastructure costs rose. Underlying earnings power was solid, but Q4 EPS overstated it slightly.
AI monetization is moving faster. Microsoft 365 Copilot paid seats surpassed 30 million, with net seat additions more than doubling quarter over quarter.
Can Microsoft’s Azure growth keep accelerating?
Demand says yes; capacity decides the pace. Microsoft has said repeatedly that customer demand exceeds supply. It added 31 datacenters in Q4 and 88 across fiscal 2026, and Hood noted that additional in-quarter capacity was quickly monetized.
The backlog supports the guide. Commercial remaining performance obligation rose 84% to $678 billion, with about 30% expected to be recognized in the next 12 months. That near-term portion, roughly $200 billion, gives Azure visibility well beyond one quarter.
The composition of that backlog is worth watching. Commercial bookings grew 18% in constant currency excluding OpenAI, but only 11% including it. That gap suggests OpenAI-related bookings were lighter in Q4 than the year before. Microsoft said sequential growth came from commitments by clients other than AI model developers, which is a healthier mix. If that broadening continues in Q1, it reduces concentration risk; if OpenAI bookings rebound, the RPO headline will rise, but so will dependence on one customer.
Is Microsoft’s capex paying off?
Not yet in cash terms. Capital expenditures, including finance leases, reached $41 billion in Q4, up 69%, and free cash flow fell to $19.6 billion. About two-thirds of that spending went to short-lived assets such as CPUs and GPUs, which depreciate faster than buildings and pressure margins sooner.
Q1 raises the stakes. Guided capex of about $50 billion is roughly $9 billion more than Q4. If operating cash flow does not grow at a similar pace, free cash flow could fall again.
Headline capex also depends on accounting. Hood kept calendar 2026 capex at about $175 billion, down from roughly $190 billion guided in April. Part of the reduction came from moving some datacenter and office leases from capital expenditures into operating leases, which shifts cost recognition rather than reducing the commitment. Investors comparing Microsoft’s capex with Alphabet’s or Amazon’s should adjust for that change.
How much does Microsoft depend on OpenAI?
Less than it did a year ago, by design. On April 27, 2026, Microsoft and OpenAI amended their partnership. Microsoft no longer pays a revenue share to OpenAI, while OpenAI’s payments to Microsoft, about 20%, continue through 2030 subject to a total cap. Microsoft’s license to OpenAI models and products runs through 2032 but is now non-exclusive, and OpenAI can serve its products on any cloud.
That amendment cuts both ways. Ending Microsoft’s outbound revenue share improves its margins. But a non-exclusive license and multi-cloud freedom mean OpenAI workloads can move to competitors over time. The earlier commitment still matters: in October 2025, OpenAI contracted to buy an incremental $250 billion of Azure services, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal as OpenAI’s compute provider.
Microsoft also books gains and losses from its OpenAI stake. In fiscal 2026, net gains from OpenAI investments added $4.96 billion to net income, or $0.67 per share. Those gains are non-operating and can swing either way, so EPS comparisons should strip them out.
Is MSFT stock fairly valued before earnings?
Microsoft trades at a premium to its own guidance, though not an extreme one. Using Morningstar’s implied Q1 EPS of $4.70, annualized earnings are about $18.80. At a share price in the low $530s, that implies roughly 28 times run-rate earnings, in line with the high-20s forward multiple many analysts cite.
That multiple reflects 16% revenue growth and 45% Azure growth at the same time. The stock was weak from late October 2025 through late June 2026 before July’s results triggered a re-rating. Holding the gain requires Microsoft to deliver on its own guide, not merely meet consensus.
Peer reports in the same week will shape expectations. Alphabet and Amazon also report around October 27–28, and their cloud growth will set the comparison for Azure.
FAQ
Q1: When does Microsoft report fiscal Q1 2027 earnings?
A1: Microsoft is expected to report fiscal Q1 2027 results after the U.S. market close on October 28, 2026; one tracker lists October 27. The confirmed date is posted on Microsoft’s investor relations website.
Q2: What is Microsoft’s Azure growth guidance?
A2: Microsoft guided Azure growth of about 45% in constant currency for fiscal Q1 2027, up from 43% in fiscal Q4 2026, and said growth should continue to accelerate through the first half of fiscal 2027.
Q3: How much is Microsoft spending on capex?
A3: Microsoft spent $41 billion on capital expenditures, including finance leases, in fiscal Q4 2026 and guided about $50 billion for fiscal Q1 2027. It expects calendar 2026 capex of about $175 billion.
Q4: What changed in Microsoft’s deal with OpenAI?
A4: Under an April 27, 2026 amendment, Microsoft stopped paying a revenue share to OpenAI, OpenAI’s payments to Microsoft continue through 2030 under a cap, and Microsoft’s IP license runs through 2032 on a non-exclusive basis.

title: Microsoft stock jumps 4% as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat
snippet: Microsoft shares rose 5% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business. Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
content:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
- Earnings per share: $4.89 adjusted vs. $4.73 expected
- Revenue: $92.28 billion vs. $90.69 billion expected
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement, with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue.
For Azure, Microsoft's finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts that she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus.
"We still have demand that exceeds supply," she said.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. "Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed," Hood said.
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues.
"In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2," she said. The delays have to do with GPU-as-a-service providers, she said.
Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it's attractive to do so, Hood said.
"We're fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our rates ratings are, and sort of we haven't been able to — we haven't yet, I would say, tapped that," she said. "And then, of course, there's other options."
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers.
Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs, and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.

title: Alphabet Earnings: Revenue Up 25%, Profit Down [2026]
snippet: Oct 29, 2026 · Alphabet earnings: Q3 2026 revenue rose 25% to $127.6B while net income fell to $26.5B. What it means for Google Cloud, Gemini and developers.
content:
Alphabet reported third-quarter revenue of $127.577 billion on October 28, 2026, a 25% jump from $102.35 billion a year earlier. Net income moved the other way. The New York Times framed the print as revenue rising while profit falls, and the numbers back that reading: net income dropped to $26.468 billion from $34.979 billion, and diluted earnings per share slid to $2.12 from $2.87.
The split matters for anyone who builds on Google’s platforms. Operating income climbed 30% to $40.576 billion, so the core business got more profitable. The hit came below the operating line and from heavy AI spending that pushed free cash flow to negative $9.065 billion. We covered the run-up in our pre-earnings futures report, and this analysis picks up with what the Alphabet earnings mean for developers, cloud buyers and coding tools.
One caution on the headline. Reports describe the profit decline in different ways, and the percentage depends on whether you use net income, net income available to common shareholders, or earnings per share. We show all three below and label our own arithmetic.
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Alphabet Q3 2026 Earnings: The Numbers at a Glance
The quarter covers the three months ended September 30, 2026. Revenue landed at $127.577 billion against an analyst estimate of $128.2 billion, according to LSEG data. 9to5Google’s earnings report carries the same headline figures. That makes it a narrow miss on the top line, even though growth hit 25%.
Operating margin expanded to 31.8% from 30.5%. In plain terms, Alphabet kept more of each sales dollar after paying for the business itself. That detail gets lost when the headline says profit fell, so it deserves space before we get to the damage lower on the income statement.
| Metric | Q3 2026 | Year earlier | Change | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $127.577 billion | $102.35 billion | Up 25% | 
| Operating income | $40.576 billion | $31.2 billion | Up 30% | 
| Operating margin | 31.8% | 30.5% | Up 1.3 points | 
| Net income | $26.468 billion | $34.979 billion | Down about 24.3% (our math) | 
| Net income to common holders | $26.170 billion | $34.979 billion | Down about 25.2% (our math) | 
| Diluted EPS | $2.12 | $2.87 | Down about 26.1% (our math) | 
| Google advertising revenue | $82.01 billion | Not in our sources | Not stated | 
| Free cash flow | Negative $9.065 billion | Not in our sources | Second straight negative quarter | 
Sundar Pichai, Alphabet’s CEO, said in a statement covered by Variety: “We had a strong quarter and are now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate.” Multiply the quarter by four and you get about $510 billion, so the claim checks out on simple arithmetic.
Why Net Income Fell While Revenue Rose 25%
Revenue and operating income both rose, so the profit decline came from somewhere else. According to the AlphaStreet transcript of the earnings call, an Alphabet executive said other income and expenses was negative $8.2 billion, driven mainly by an unrealized loss on the company’s investment in SpaceX after a drop in its stock price during the third quarter. The same executive said net income and earnings per share fell because of that line.
In the executive’s words from the call: “Other income and expenses was negative $8.2 billion due primarily to unrealized loss from our investment in SpaceX from a decline in its stock price in the 3rd quarter.” The transcript file we pulled does not name the speaker, so we attribute it to an Alphabet executive on the call.
That framing changes how readers should treat the drop. A mark-to-market loss on a stake in another company is a paper item that can reverse if the stock recovers. It tells you little about whether Search, YouTube or Cloud earned less. Our SpaceX 10-Q breakdown shows how much outside scrutiny that company now draws, which helps explain why its share price can swing a big Alphabet line item.
| Measure | Q3 2026 | Year earlier | Direction | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Operating income | $40.576 billion | $31.2 billion | Up 30% | 
| Net income | $26.468 billion | $34.979 billion | Down | 
| Net income available to common shareholders | $26.170 billion | $34.979 billion | Down | 
| Diluted earnings per share | $2.12 | $2.87 | Down | 
| Other income and expenses | Negative $8.2 billion | Not in our sources | Main drag, per the call | 
The gap between operating income and net income is the story of the quarter. If you strip the investment mark out of your mental model, Alphabet looks like a company whose operating profit grew faster than its revenue. Put it back in, and shareholders saw a smaller bottom line than last year.
Google Cloud Revenue Doubles to About $31 Billion
The loudest positive number was Google Cloud. Fortune reported that Cloud revenue doubled to $31 billion while cash flow stayed deep in the red. CNBC reported Cloud revenue of $30.7 billion, up over 100%, another report puts the growth rate at 103%, and The Information lists the same $30.7 billion. We use “about $31 billion” and flag that the exact number varies by outlet.
Doubling a business that size in one year is rare. A year ago the unit brought in $15.157 billion, roughly half of this quarter’s figure, which means Google added about $15 billion of quarterly Cloud revenue in twelve months. The Information said demand from AI customers powered the surge.
For developers, Cloud is the part of Alphabet you pay. Gemini API calls, GPU and TPU capacity, managed Kubernetes and storage all roll up here. A unit that doubles is a unit that is signing large contracts, hiring sales engineers and shipping new services at speed. It also tends to be a unit that raises prices once capacity tightens.
Compare that with the picture at Microsoft and Amazon. Our Amazon and Microsoft earnings preview listed consensus revenue of $202.16 billion for Amazon and $90.63 billion for Microsoft. Alphabet’s Cloud number is smaller than either parent total, yet its growth rate is the part rivals will study first.
TPU Sales and the Chip Business Behind Cloud Growth
The Information reported that sales of Google’s Tensor Processing Unit AI chips contributed meaningfully to Cloud growth. It also reported on Monday, before the results, that Google had struck a deal to sell TPUs to OpenAI. Pichai said Google expects the vast majority of TPU revenue to arrive in 2027, according to the same outlet.
That timing shapes the next several quarters. If the largest TPU revenue lands in 2027, then 2026 looks like the build-out year, with spending up front and sales later. It fits a quarter where cash flow turned deeply negative while Cloud revenue ran ahead of plan.
The strategic shift is easy to miss. Google used to treat its custom silicon mostly as an internal advantage for Search, YouTube and its own models. Selling TPU systems to outside AI labs turns that advantage into a product line, and it puts Google in more direct competition with Nvidia and AMD. That shelf is already crowded.
Free Cash Flow Slips to Negative $9.065 Billion
Free cash flow was negative $9.065 billion. The Information noted this is the second straight quarter of negative free cash flow, and a big step down from negative $5.9 billion in the prior quarter. In round numbers, the deficit grew by about $3.2 billion in 90 days.
CNBC’s coverage also cited analyst expectations near negative $2.7 billion, which would make the actual print far weaker than forecast. We treat that expectation as a secondary data point because we could not confirm it against a primary filing. The direction is not in doubt either way.
Why does a company with a 31.8% operating margin burn cash? Because building data centers, buying accelerators and laying networking gear costs money before the matching revenue shows up. Operating income counts depreciation over many years, while free cash flow counts the check written today. When spending jumps, the two measures drift apart fast.
Alphabet is not alone. Our report on Meta’s $33.9 billion capex topping cash flow described the same squeeze, and reports say Meta has gone further by targeting a $95 billion stock raise. Investors now ask every hyperscaler the same question: how long can spending outrun cash?
Capex at $51.36 Billion and a $195 Billion to $205 Billion Plan
According to CNBC’s earnings coverage, Alphabet spent about $51.36 billion on capital expenditures in the quarter, below the roughly $55.09 billion analysts expected. The company held its full-year 2026 capex forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion. A lower-than-expected spend in one quarter did not change the annual plan, and Alphabet said it expects a significant increase in 2027 capital spending.
Do the math on the guide. Spread evenly across four quarters, $195 billion to $205 billion works out to roughly $49 billion to $51 billion a quarter, so the Q3 pace sits right on the plan and points to another heavy fourth quarter. Against $127.577 billion of quarterly revenue, $51.36 billion of capex equals about 40% of sales by our calculation.
Our broader roundup of a $1.7 trillion backlog against $600 billion of capex frames the bet. The backlog says customers have signed up for the capacity. The capex says the bill arrives first. Alphabet’s quarter fits that pattern exactly.
Search and Ads: $82.01 Billion and a Slower Services Pace
Google advertising revenue came in at $82.01 billion. That is about 64% of total quarterly revenue by our calculation, so ads still carry the company. CNBC reported that Google search revenue rose 12% to $63.35 billion. The Information reported that Google’s services business, which includes core Search advertising, grew less than 11% in the quarter, its slowest rate since the first quarter of last year.
Read those two facts together. Total revenue grew 25% while services grew under 11%, which means Cloud and other lines supplied much of the gap. Ads remain huge but no longer set the growth rate for the group. That is the clearest structural change in this report. Subscriptions add a second leg, since Alphabet said YouTube Music and Premium surpassed 150M subscribers in October 2026.
The Manila Times, relaying wire reports, said shares plummeted on a profit miss and an ad slowdown. Whether the ad slowdown reflects AI answers eating into clicks or just a tough comparison is something the sources do not settle. Treat any confident claim on that point as opinion.
Gemini Reaches 1 Billion Users and Gemini 4 Carbon Lands
CNBC’s coverage says the Gemini app reached 1 billion users, a milestone Alphabet described as the fastest growth of any product in its history. On the same day as the results, The Information reported that Google released Gemini 4 Carbon, which it described as significantly more capable than Argon, a model that Carbon followed by 2 weeks. Carbon was announced on October 28 and reportedly started with a limited rollout to selected cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program. On November 10, 2026 it became available beyond initial security testers to paying developers, businesses and Google AI Ultra subscribers, including in the Gemini app, and Google positions it as its strongest model for long-horizon engineering and cybersecurity.
A model cadence measured in weeks creates real work for engineering teams. Each release can change output quality, latency, cost per token and tool-calling behavior. Our Gemini 4 Carbon benchmark report covers the published scores, including 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, so we will not repeat them here.
The pairing of a 1 billion user milestone with a fresh flagship model is deliberate. It tells Wall Street that the spending buys a product people use and a model that keeps improving. It tells developers that the Gemini API is not going to sit still.
Gemini 4 Argon Pricing and API Usage
Gemini 4 Argon reportedly became generally available on October 13, 2026, and Gemini 4 Carbon was announced on October 28, 2026 as Alphabet’s next frontier model, with a limited rollout so far. Google’s own pages list the introductory price for Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026, rising to $4 and $20 on December 1, 2026. For teams that call the API from production code, that price step is the most direct thing to plan around when keeping a bill under control.
The introductory rate has an end date. After the introductory period expires on November 30, 2026, the price of $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens will apply, and Google says this applies to the Argon model intended for public access only. Anyone who budgeted around the lower rate should re-run their cost estimates at the higher listed price before the change takes effect on December 1, 2026.
Demand is already heavy. Google said its Gemini APIs processed 32B tokens per minute in October 2026, over 4× October 2025. Advertisers are leaning on the same models: according to Alphabet, Google advertisers generated 1.5B AI campaign assets in October 2026, up over 7× year over year. Read together, the usage figures and the price schedule explain why this earnings report matters to developers. Usage is climbing fast, the listed rate is scheduled to rise once the introductory period ends, and Alphabet has told investors it is spending heavily to add capacity. Teams should track token consumption per feature, test whether a cheaper model handles routine requests, and treat the end of the introductory period as a budgeting deadline rather than a surprise.
What the Results Mean for Developers and Coding Tools
Alphabet did not break out coding products in the figures we reviewed, so no one can say how much of Cloud’s doubling came from AI-assisted coding. What the results do show is the infrastructure that coding tools run on. Every code-completion, review or agent product needs inference capacity, and Google just told investors it is adding that capacity at a pace of roughly $200 billion a year.
Capacity should help, pricing pressure may follow
More TPU and GPU supply tends to ease rate limits and queue times for API customers. At the same time, negative free cash flow gives Alphabet a reason to push for returns on that spending. Developers who built on cheap tokens should watch for changes in tiers, committed-use discounts and bundling with Workspace or Cloud contracts.
Model churn is now a maintenance cost
With Argon and Carbon arriving 2 weeks apart, teams that pin a model version need a regression harness. Our guide to piloting AI coding assistants with a team covers the human side of the same problem.
TPU access could widen the hardware menu
If Google sells TPU systems to outside labs, as The Information reports it has agreed to do for OpenAI, then more AI workloads will run on a non-Nvidia stack. Framework support for TPUs matters more as that happens. Teams that write portable training and serving code gain bargaining power, while teams locked to one vendor lose it.
| Signal | What Alphabet reported | Why developers care | 
|---|---|---|
| Google Cloud revenue | About $31 billion, roughly double year over year | Faster product launches, but tighter capacity can lift prices | 
| TPU sales | Meaningful contribution, most revenue expected in 2027 | More non-Nvidia options for training and inference | 
| Gemini app users | 1 billion, per CNBC | Large installed base for Gemini-powered features | 
| Newest model | Gemini 4 Hydrogen, announced November 12, 2026, after Gemini 4 Carbon | Frequent upgrades demand regression testing | 
| Free cash flow | Negative $9.065 billion | Pressure to monetize developer products sooner | 
| Capex | $51.36 billion in Q3, $195 billion to $205 billion guided for 2026 | Capacity growth that should ease rate limits over time | 
Market Reaction: Shares Drop Nearly 9% After Hours
The Information reported that Alphabet’s shares fell nearly 9% in after-hours trading. The Winnipeg Free Press said the stock sank in early after-hours action after Google missed Wall Street expectations. Chosun’s English edition headlined that the 25% revenue jump on AI fell short of forecasts.
Three misses drove the move, based on the reporting: revenue slightly under the $128.2 billion estimate, earnings per share well under analyst hopes, and cash flow far weaker than forecast. A strong Cloud print was not enough to offset them. Investors who bought on the AI story wanted proof that spending turns into profit and cash, and this quarter gave them proof of revenue only.
After-hours moves can fade or deepen once the regular session opens and analysts publish notes. We have no confirmed regular-session close in our sources, so we stop at the after-hours figure.
How Alphabet Compares With Microsoft, Amazon and Meta
Each large cloud player is running the same experiment at a different scale. Microsoft and Amazon carry the biggest absolute cloud businesses, and our earlier preview put consensus revenue at $90.63 billion and $202.16 billion for the two parents. Meta sells no cloud capacity, so its capex has to pay off through ads and products, which is why its $33.9 billion quarterly figure drew attention.
Alphabet sits in an unusual middle position. It has a mature ad machine, a fast-growing cloud unit, its own AI chips and a frontier model family. That vertical stack is the bull case, since Google controls more of its cost structure than a company that rents chips from others. It is also the bear case, because Google carries the capex risk of all four layers at once.
On growth, Alphabet’s 25% total revenue increase and roughly doubled Cloud line stand out. On cash, it looks weaker than the pre-spend era of the business. The open question is whether every competitor can sustain this pace at once.
Historical Context: From Ad Machine to AI Infrastructure Landlord
For most of Alphabet’s life, the company funded everything from Search advertising and returned cash to shareholders. Cloud was the junior business. This quarter flips part of that script. A year earlier Alphabet posted net income of $34.979 billion and operating income of $31.2 billion. Now operating income is $40.576 billion, but the business consumed cash.
The year-earlier base also explains why the revenue comparison looks so large. Revenue rose by about $25.2 billion in twelve months, from $102.35 billion to $127.577 billion.
Our readers who track platform shifts will recognize the pattern. When a company moves from selling software and ads to renting infrastructure, margins and cash flow follow a different rhythm. Spending leads, revenue follows, and the market punishes the gap in between.
Expert Voices From the Earnings Call
We limited direct quotes to statements we could verify against the call transcript and company commentary. Pichai said the company is on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate, as reported by Variety. On the call, an Alphabet executive said consolidated revenues were $127.6 billion, up 25% in both reported and constant currency, according to the AlphaStreet transcript.
The constant-currency point is useful. It tells us the 25% growth was not a foreign-exchange artifact, because the reported and constant-currency growth rates matched. An executive also said that net income and earnings per share decreased due to the decline in other income and expenses. That is the company’s own explanation, and it lines up with the SpaceX investment loss described earlier.
Outside analysts split on how to read it. Wire coverage emphasized the revenue and cash flow misses, while Fortune stressed that Cloud revenue doubled. Both readings fit the data. We did not find a named analyst quote we could verify, so we leave the debate to the numbers.
Five Predictions for the Next Two Quarters
The following are our analysis, not reported facts. They rest on the figures above and carry real uncertainty.
- Free cash flow stays negative in Q4. A $195 billion to $205 billion annual capex guide implies a pace near Q3’s $51.36 billion, and that spending lands before the matching revenue.
- Cloud growth stays above 50%. Doubling again from a larger base is unlikely, but TPU deals and AI demand should keep growth high.
- Gemini API pricing gets more tiers. Negative cash flow gives Alphabet a reason to segment pricing between cheap models and the newest flagship.
- Another Gemini release lands within a quarter. A gap of 2 weeks between Argon and Carbon suggests the cadence will not slow.
- The SpaceX mark swings the next print. If its stock recovers, other income and expenses could flip and lift net income without any operating change.
Readers who want the broader software angle can browse our software coverage hub for tool comparisons that connect to these shifts.
Three items will move the story before the next report. First, any filing detail that breaks out Cloud operating income, because Cloud profit matters as much as Cloud revenue. RTTNews headlined that profit fell despite 25% revenue growth while Cloud revenue doubled, which captures the tension in one line.
Second, TPU contract disclosures. Pichai said most TPU revenue lands in 2027, so look for backlog or customer commitments that confirm it. Third, capex guidance for next year. Investors will want a credible path from spending to free cash flow.
For engineering leads, the practical step is simpler. Review your cloud contracts, pin model versions, and keep a second provider tested and ready. Google ships new models fast, and this quarter’s cash numbers give the company strong reasons to keep that pace.
FAQ: Alphabet Q3 2026 Earnings
How much did Alphabet earn in Q3 2026?
Alphabet reported revenue of $127.577 billion and net income of $26.468 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. Net income available to common shareholders was $26.170 billion, and diluted earnings per share were $2.12.
Why did Alphabet’s profit fall if revenue rose 25%?
Operating income rose 30% to $40.576 billion. According to the earnings call transcript, the decline came from other income and expenses of negative $8.2 billion, driven mainly by an unrealized loss on the SpaceX investment.
By how much did profit fall?
It depends on the measure. By our arithmetic, net income fell about 24.3%, net income to common shareholders fell about 25.2%, and diluted EPS fell about 26.1%. The headline’s wording of a 25% profit drop does not match any single reported figure exactly.
How big is Google Cloud now?
Fortune reported about $31 billion in Cloud revenue, roughly double the year-earlier figure. The Information gave $30.7 billion, and another report cited 103% growth.
Did Alphabet miss analyst estimates?
Revenue of $127.577 billion fell just short of the $128.2 billion LSEG estimate. Reports also describe weaker earnings and cash flow than analysts expected, and shares fell nearly 9% after hours, according to The Information.
What does this mean for developers using Gemini or Google Cloud?
Expect more capacity and faster model releases, with Gemini 4 Carbon arriving 2 weeks after Argon. Also expect pressure on Alphabet to monetize, so watch pricing tiers and test each new model before you upgrade production workloads.
What is Alphabet’s capex plan for 2026?
CNBC’s coverage says Alphabet held its full-year forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion after spending about $51.36 billion in the third quarter.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Revenue | $127.577 billion | $102.35 billion | Up 25% |

title: Google Business Strategy 2026: AI, Search, Cloud & Revenue Diversification - The Strategy Story
snippet: Google Search and advertising remain the financial foundation. In fiscal 2025, Alphabet generated $402.8 billion in revenue, including $294.7 billion from Google advertising. At the same time, faster-growing businesses such as Google Cloud, subscriptions and AI are becoming increasingly important.
content:
Alphabet’s business strategy in 2026 is increasingly centered on a transition from an advertising-led internet company toward a full-stack AI and technology platform company.
Google Search and advertising remain the financial foundation. In fiscal 2025, Alphabet generated $402.8 billion in revenue, including $294.7 billion from Google advertising. At the same time, faster-growing businesses such as Google Cloud, subscriptions and AI are becoming increasingly important. Google Cloud revenue reached $58.7 billion, while Google subscriptions, platforms and devices generated $48.0 billion.
Alphabet itself identifies several long-term trends shaping its strategy: expanding AI across products, increasing revenue beyond advertising, investing heavily in technical infrastructure, and continuing R&D, acquisitions and strategic investments.
Based strictly on Alphabet’s 2025 Form 10-K, five major strategic pillars define Google’s business strategy in 2026.
Google Business Model 2026: How Does Alphabet Make Money?
1. Making AI the Foundation Across Google’s Entire Product Portfolio
The most important pillar of Alphabet’s strategy is artificial intelligence.
Google has described itself as an AI-first company since 2016. In 2026, however, AI is no longer simply a research initiative or an additional feature. Alphabet is building what it calls a full-stack AI approach spanning infrastructure, research, frontier models, developer tools and consumer and enterprise applications.
At the infrastructure level, Google uses specialized GPUs and its own custom-designed Tensor Processing Units. Its seventh-generation TPU, Ironwood, is part of an infrastructure strategy designed to support Google’s own products and Google Cloud customers.
At the model layer sits Gemini. Alphabet reported that all 15 of its products with more than 500 million users—including seven with more than two billion users—were already using Gemini models. Gemini is being incorporated into Search, the Gemini app, Google Workspace and Google Cloud.
This gives Alphabet an important strategic advantage: it can distribute AI through products that already have enormous user bases.
Rather than needing to build entirely new distribution for AI, Google can integrate it into existing services.
Search is being transformed through AI Overviews and AI Mode. AI Overviews provides synthesized responses to queries, while AI Mode uses Gemini’s reasoning and multimodal capabilities to handle more complex questions that might historically have required several searches.
The same strategy extends to enterprises. Gemini Enterprise and Gemini for Google Workspace bring AI agents and generative AI into business workflows, while Vertex AI enables customers to build their own AI applications.
Alphabet acknowledges that monetization may evolve as these AI experiences develop. The company says it generally focuses first on the user experience and then on monetization, while noting that AI could alter both revenue growth and margin trends.
The underlying strategy is therefore:
Build frontier AI → control AI infrastructure → integrate Gemini across major products → distribute AI to billions of users → monetize across advertising, subscriptions and enterprise cloud.
2. Defending and Reinventing Search and Advertising
Despite the rapid expansion of AI, advertising remains the economic engine funding Alphabet’s broader strategy.
Google advertising generated $294.7 billion in fiscal 2025, representing more than 70% of Alphabet’s total revenue. Search & other alone contributed $224.5 billion, while YouTube advertising generated $40.4 billion and Google Network $29.8 billion.
Alphabet therefore cannot simply replace traditional Search with AI without considering the economics of advertising.
Its strategy is instead to reinvent Search while protecting advertiser value.
Google Search revenue increased by $26.4 billion in 2025, supported by higher search queries, greater mobile adoption and usage, increased advertiser spending, and improvements in ad formats and delivery.
The underlying advertising model has two major components.
Performance advertising connects advertisers to users with the objective of producing measurable actions or conversions.
Brand advertising helps advertisers increase awareness through video, images, text and other interactive formats.
AI increasingly supports both.
Alphabet states that AI has been foundational to its advertising business for more than a decade, with products such as Performance Max, Demand Gen and Product Studio using AI to identify additional conversion opportunities.
Alphabet is also improving monetization efficiency.
For Google Search & other properties, paid clicks increased 6% while cost-per-click increased 7% in 2025. On Google Network properties, impressions declined 7% while cost-per-impression increased 7%.
The strategic challenge is significant because AI is changing how users obtain information.
Alphabet recognizes that user engagement with AI could require different monetization models from historical Search experiences. But its enormous advertising infrastructure, advertiser relationships and distribution provide an existing economic system through which new AI-based search formats can potentially be monetized.
The objective is therefore not merely to defend the traditional “ten blue links” model. It is to move Search into a new AI-driven interface while preserving its value to users and advertisers.
3. Building Google Cloud Into Alphabet’s Second Major Growth Engine
The third strategic pillar is Google Cloud.
Cloud is strategically important because it allows Alphabet to monetize the same infrastructure, AI models and technical capabilities developed internally for Google products with enterprise customers.
Google Cloud revenue increased from $43.2 billion in 2024 to $58.7 billion in 2025, growth of approximately 36%. Operating income increased from $6.1 billion to $13.9 billion, meaning Cloud is becoming both a major growth engine and an increasingly meaningful contributor to profitability.
Google Cloud’s strategy operates across several layers.
At the infrastructure layer, Google provides compute, AI accelerators, storage and networking.
At the AI-development layer, Vertex AI allows customers to access, tune and deploy more than 200 foundation models, including Gemini, third-party models and open models.
At the application layer, Google Workspace provides Gmail, Docs, Calendar, Drive and Meet, increasingly integrated with Gemini.
Google Cloud also provides data analytics, cybersecurity and enterprise AI agents.
This multi-layer strategy is important because Alphabet can monetize AI at several points in the enterprise technology stack.
A company can pay Google for infrastructure to train models, for Vertex AI to build applications, for Gemini Enterprise to deploy agents and for Workspace subscriptions through which employees use AI.
Alphabet’s $242.8 billion revenue backlog, primarily related to Google Cloud, further demonstrates the increasing scale of this enterprise business. Just over half of that backlog is expected to be recognized within 24 months.
Alphabet is also strengthening Cloud through acquisitions.
In 2025, the company agreed to acquire cybersecurity platform Wiz for $32 billion, with the transaction expected to close in 2026 subject to approvals. Alphabet states that Wiz will become part of Google Cloud.
The deal reinforces cybersecurity as a strategic component of Google Cloud rather than treating Cloud solely as infrastructure.
4. Diversifying Revenue Beyond Advertising Through Subscriptions, Platforms and Devices
Alphabet’s fourth strategic priority is increasing the proportion of revenue that comes from businesses other than advertising.
The company explicitly states that cloud, consumer subscriptions, platforms and devices have grown over time, with some growing faster than advertising and becoming a larger share of consolidated revenue. Alphabet expects this trend to continue.
Google subscriptions, platforms and devices revenue increased from $40.3 billion in 2024 to $48.0 billion in 2025, growth of approximately 19%.
The increase was primarily driven by paid subscriptions across YouTube services and Google One.
This category provides three different diversification mechanisms.
Consumer Subscriptions
YouTube TV, YouTube Music and Premium, NFL Sunday Ticket and Google One create direct recurring relationships with customers.
Google One is particularly important to the AI strategy because it includes access to Google’s most capable Gemini models.
Platform Revenue
Google Play allows Alphabet to monetize sales of applications and in-app purchases.
Devices
Pixel smartphones and other devices allow Google to combine its AI, software and hardware.
Alphabet describes the strategic potential of devices as combining the best of its AI, software and hardware, citing products such as the Pixel 10 series and Pixel Watch 4.
The diversification strategy does come with a financial trade-off.
Alphabet notes that revenues from cloud, subscriptions, platforms and devices generally have lower margins than advertising.
Alphabet therefore appears willing to accept some mix shift in margins in exchange for broader revenue sources and participation in new technology markets.
5. Investing Aggressively in Infrastructure, R&D, Acquisitions and Moonshots
Alphabet’s fifth strategic pillar is aggressive long-term capital allocation.
AI changes the physical requirements of Alphabet’s business.
Historically, Search and advertising were highly scalable software businesses. Modern generative AI requires substantially more servers, accelerators, energy, networking and datacenter capacity.
Alphabet spent $91.4 billion on capital expenditures in 2025, primarily on technical infrastructure. The company expects to increase technical-infrastructure investment significantly again in 2026, including spending on servers, network equipment and datacenters.
Alphabet acknowledges that AI will increase depreciation, energy, equipment and network-capacity expenses because training and serving AI models require more computing power than its historical products.
The company is trying to offset part of that increase through datacenter efficiencies and its own TPU architecture.
R&D is another major component.
Alphabet spent $61.1 billion on research and development in 2025, up from $49.3 billion in 2024. R&D therefore represented approximately 15% of revenue.
Alphabet explicitly states that R&D, acquisitions and strategic investments remain important elements of its capital allocation strategy because they expand its technology capabilities, engineering expertise and strategic partnerships.
Two major announced acquisitions demonstrate that approach.
The proposed $32 billion Wiz acquisition strengthens Google Cloud cybersecurity.
The proposed $4.8 billion acquisition of Intersect, a data-center and energy-infrastructure company, supports infrastructure expansion. Both were expected to close in 2026 subject to regulatory approvals.
Alphabet is also continuing to fund longer-term “moonshots.”
Waymo is already providing fully autonomous paid ride-hailing services and is expanding commercially. In February 2026, Waymo announced a $16 billion investment round, the significant majority of which was funded by Alphabet.
Other Bets nevertheless produced a $7.5 billion operating loss in 2025.
The strategic logic is that the highly profitable Google Services business gives Alphabet the financial capacity to fund technologies that may take years to become commercially significant.
What Is the Core of Google’s Business Strategy?
Google’s business strategy in 2026 can be summarized as a transition from organizing and monetizing information to building and monetizing intelligence across the technology stack.
Its five strategic pillars are:
- Make Gemini and AI foundational across Search, YouTube, Cloud, Workspace and other products.
- Reinvent Search and advertising for the AI era while protecting Google’s largest profit engine.
- Scale Google Cloud into a second major revenue and profit engine.
- Diversify beyond advertising through subscriptions, digital platforms and devices.
- Invest aggressively in AI infrastructure, R&D, acquisitions and long-term technology bets.
These pillars reinforce one another.
Google Services gives Alphabet billions of users and enormous cash generation.
That cash finances AI research and infrastructure.
AI improves Search and advertising while creating new consumer experiences.
The same AI technology can be sold through Google Cloud.
Subscriptions create direct customer monetization.
Custom TPUs lower dependence on a purely third-party AI infrastructure model.
Other Bets provide exposure to future markets such as autonomous transportation.
The result is a vertically connected strategy extending from physical datacenters and processors all the way to consumer and enterprise applications.
Financial Evidence Behind Google’s Strategy
Alphabet’s fiscal 2025 results show the shift clearly.
| Business | FY2024 revenue | FY2025 revenue | Approx. growth | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Google advertising | $264.6B | $294.7B | 11% | 
| Subscriptions, platforms & devices | $40.3B | $48.0B | 19% | 
| Google Cloud | $43.2B | $58.7B | 36% | 
| Alphabet total | $350.0B | $402.8B | 15% | 
The strategic diversification is evident.
Advertising remains dominant, but Cloud and direct consumer monetization are growing considerably faster.
Profitability is also improving outside Google’s core advertising model.
Google Cloud operating income increased from $6.1 billion to $13.9 billion, while Google Services generated $139.4 billion of operating income.
At the same time, Alphabet is spending aggressively to prepare for the next technology cycle.
Capital expenditures reached $91.4 billion and R&D reached $61.1 billion in 2025. Combined, those two figures illustrate the extraordinary amount of capital Alphabet is directing toward technology development and infrastructure.
The Strategic Trade-Off: AI Growth Versus Capital Intensity
Alphabet’s AI strategy also creates a major trade-off.
The company wants AI to increase engagement, improve its products and create new revenue sources. But generative AI requires significantly greater infrastructure investment than many traditional Google products.
Alphabet expects depreciation, energy, equipment and network costs to increase significantly as AI workloads expand.
The company’s technical infrastructure also carries large contractual commitments. At the end of 2025, Alphabet had $149.1 billion of purchase commitments and other contractual obligations, including energy arrangements, licenses and technical-infrastructure and inventory orders.
This means success in AI will depend not only on building superior models.
Alphabet also needs to convert massive infrastructure spending into enough additional advertising, cloud and subscription revenue to justify the capital intensity.
That is becoming one of the most important economic questions surrounding its strategy.
Conclusion
Google’s business strategy in 2026 is built around AI-led transformation without abandoning the economic strength of its existing platforms.
Search and advertising remain the financial core, generating nearly $295 billion in advertising revenue during fiscal 2025. Rather than replacing that model, Alphabet is integrating AI into Search and advertising in an attempt to preserve user relevance while evolving the way information is discovered and monetized.
At the same time, Google Cloud is emerging as a second major business engine. Revenue grew approximately 36% to $58.7 billion, while operating income more than doubled to $13.9 billion.
Subscriptions, platforms and devices add another layer of diversification, reaching $48.0 billion in revenue.
Underneath all of these businesses is increasingly the same technology stack: datacenters, GPUs and TPUs → frontier Gemini models → developer platforms → consumer and enterprise applications → multiple monetization models.
Alphabet is spending heavily to build that stack. Capital expenditure reached $91.4 billion and R&D spending reached $61.1 billion in 2025, while acquisitions such as Wiz and Intersect are designed to strengthen cloud security and infrastructure capabilities.
The larger strategic direction is therefore clear: Alphabet is attempting to use the cash flows and distribution of Google’s existing businesses to become one of the dominant full-stack platforms of the AI era.
Source: Google Annual Report

title: Musk “Would Never Lend Money” to Pure AI Clouds. Goldman Is Selling SpaceX’s $40 Billion GPU Debt
snippet: Key TakeawaysGoldman Sachs and Apollo are marketing slices of a roughly $40 billion debt package that buys Nvidia chips for ...
content:
Goldman Sachs and Apollo are marketing slices of a roughly $40 billion debt package that buys Nvidia chips for SpaceX to rent, Bloomberg reported.
Elon Musk says he would never lend to a company that only makes money serving AI from a data center, and this deal is written so lenders can count on all of SpaceX, Starlink included, to pay the rent.
The chips will earn compute revenue: SpaceX's AI segment brought in more than half of its third-quarter sales, and analysts expect total revenue to reach $336 billion in 2028.
The debt should find buyers on SpaceX's credit, but shareholders carry the neocloud risk, so the price the bonds sell at is the number to watch.
Goldman Sachs (GS:NYSE) and Apollo Global Management (APO:NYSE) are shopping pieces of a roughly $40 billion chip financing for SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ), Bloomberg reported on Nov. 4. The money buys Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) chips that SpaceX will rent for its AI data centers.
That sits awkwardly next to Elon Musk's own lending rule. Dave Blundin, a regular on Moonshots with Peter Diamandis, read Musk's line back on the show's Nov. 4 episode:
"I would never lend money to somebody who only makes money by serving AI from a data center."
It's why Musk expects death and consolidation for neoclouds as debt markets shut. But SemiAnalysis' Dylan Patel put SpaceX itself in that camp on TBPN a day earlier: "He's taking SpaceX and turning it into a NeoCloud, right? In some sense, right?"
So who's right? Goldman and Apollo's buyers are about to weigh in.
TIKR tracks 39 analysts on SpaceX. How many say "Buy"?
See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on SpaceX, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See SpaceX's Analyst Ratings
Half of SpaceX's sales already come from AI
Patel has a point. SpaceX's AI segment brought in $7.56 billion of its $14.6 billion of third-quarter revenue, nearly triple the second quarter's $2.56 billion, mostly on cloud contracts.
Analysts expect total revenue to climb steeply from here:
Getting to $336 billion in 2028 means renting out far more compute, and this debt is how SpaceX plans to pay for it. Morgan Stanley's $300 target puts $165 on enterprise AI and $118 on connectivity, Starlink included.
SpaceX owes the rent no matter what
A special purpose vehicle managed by Apollo-backed Atlas SP buys the chips and issues the debt. Bloomberg says the structure keeps it off SpaceX's balance sheet. The debt and a $7 billion lease prepayment pay for about $47.3 billion of Nvidia's latest Rubin chips, due in the first half of 2027.
SpaceX rents them for five years, and its marketing presentation reportedly says the rent is owed whatever happens to the equipment, force majeure included.
So these lenders are counting on all of SpaceX, Starlink and launches included. That's Musk's rule at work.
The catch: SpaceX owes five years of rent, but its biggest customer can leave sooner. Bloomberg identified Anthropic as the source of 34.5% of third-quarter revenue. Either side can end that contract on 90 days' notice after its first three months.
SpaceX's debt was already climbing, too:
Debt and finance leases reached $38.8 billion by Sept. 30, up from $22.9 billion at the end of 2025. Yet SpaceX's own filing calls this deal a master finance lease. If it lands on that line too, $40 billion would more than double it.
Starlink can't pay for all of this
Starlink makes SpaceX a good credit by Musk's standard: Connectivity earned $5.21 billion from operations in the first nine months, while space and AI lost a combined $4.51 billion.
But the data-center build costs far more than Starlink earns:
Free cash flow was -$10.0 billion in the third quarter alone. Morgan Stanley doesn't see it turning positive until 2031, and it expects $390 billion of outside borrowing along the way.
So this $40 billion is just the start.
Selling the loan down is routine
Goldman reportedly led an $8.3 billion senior-secured loan that goes to other banks, and Apollo was the key investor in the bonds headed to asset managers. Banks arrange deals like this to sell them, so the sale itself says little.
The backdrop is less routine. Investors agreed to the package before it priced, which left them exposed as lenders turned against neoclouds such as CoreWeave.
Blundin's version of Musk's pitch is that lenders should skip the other AI clouds at 15% and lend to SpaceX at about 8%. If these bonds price near the low end, buyers see SpaceX. Near the high end, they see Patel's neocloud.
The way I see it, this debt sells, because the deal hands lenders SpaceX's credit. Shareholders get no such cushion: more than half of Morgan Stanley's $300 target sits on the AI business, the part Musk says he'd never lend to on its own. I'd want to see where these bonds price before paying up for that.
Of course, the Rubin chips don't arrive until the first half of 2027, and SpaceX's fourth-quarter results early next year will show how much cash its $35 billion to $40 billion capex quarter used.

title: How Meta Makes Money: Ad Auctions, ARPU Geography, and the Reality Labs Bet | PitchGrade Research
snippet: Mar 11, 2026 · In 2025, Meta generated approximately $165–170 billion in revenue — roughly 98% from advertising — while burning ~$17–20 billion annually through Reality Labs, its augmented and virtual reality division.
content:
How Meta Makes Money: Ad Auctions, ARPU Geography, and the Reality Labs Bet
Executive Summary
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) is, at its core, a two-sided attention marketplace with one of the most sophisticated real-time pricing engines ever built. In 2025, Meta generated approximately $165–170 billion in revenue — roughly 98% from advertising — while burning ~$17–20 billion annually through Reality Labs, its augmented and virtual reality division. The stock has recovered dramatically from its 2022 trough (~$88) to trade above $600 as of early 2026, reflecting a market that has largely accepted that the ad business is structurally sound and that Reality Labs is a long-duration option, not an existential threat.
This article dissects exactly how that ad machine works, why average revenue per user (ARPU) varies by a factor of nearly 20x between geographies, what the unit economics look like at 3.3 billion daily active users, and whether the Reality Labs bet is rational capital allocation or the largest vanity project in corporate history.
The Business Model in Plain English
Meta owns the four largest social applications in the world by daily active users: Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. It monetizes this attention through a real-time advertising auction — specifically a second-price Vickrey-style auction with quality adjustments — that runs billions of times per day across its surfaces.
Here is the mechanism in plain English:
- Advertisers submit bids — a maximum willingness to pay per outcome (click, impression, conversion, app install).
- Meta's system calculates an effective CPM for each ad unit, weighting the advertiser's bid against a predicted action rate (the probability a specific user takes the desired action) and an estimated ad quality score.
- The winning advertiser pays not their full bid, but the minimum amount necessary to beat the next-best alternative — with adjustments for quality.
- This means Meta's revenue is a direct function of three variables: number of ad slots × fill rate × price per slot, where price per slot is itself a function of competition among advertisers.
What makes this model remarkable is that Meta doesn't just sell eyeballs — it sells predicted outcomes. Its competitive moat is the feedback loop: more users generate more behavioral data, which improves prediction accuracy, which raises effective CPMs, which attracts more advertiser spend, which funds more product development to retain users. This flywheel has been running since roughly 2012.
Revenue Streams Breakdown
| Revenue Source | Approx. 2025 Contribution | Notes | 
|---|---|---|
| Advertising (Family of Apps) | ~98% | Facebook, Instagram, Reels, Messenger, WhatsApp | 
| Reality Labs (hardware + software) | ~1–2% | Ray-Ban Meta glasses, Quest headsets, Horizon Worlds | 
| Other (payments, WhatsApp Business API) | <1% | Small but growing in emerging markets | 
Advertising Subsegments
Within advertising, the mix has shifted materially:
- Instagram now accounts for an estimated 40–45% of total ad revenue, having overtaken Facebook's News Feed as the primary monetization surface. Reels advertising on Instagram has scaled from near-zero in 2022 to a meaningful contributor.
- Facebook (News Feed, Stories, Marketplace) contributes approximately 45–50%.
- WhatsApp and Messenger remain underpenetrated. WhatsApp Business API (charging businesses per message) is a real revenue line in Brazil, India, and Southeast Asia, but it is pre-scale relative to the opportunity.
- Threads, launched in 2023, has not been monetized aggressively as of early 2026 — Meta has been deliberate about not repeating the mistake of prioritizing short-term ad load over product quality.
Reality Labs
Reality Labs lost approximately $17–19 billion in 2025 (the division has lost cumulatively over $50 billion since breaking out as a separate segment in 2021). Revenue is in the low single-digit billions, driven by Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses — which have been a genuine consumer hit at a ~$300 price point — and Quest 3/3S headset sales. This is not a profitable business. It is a funded research program.
Unit Economics
ARPU: The Geographic Fracture
This is where Meta's business model reveals its greatest structural complexity. ARPU is not uniform — it reflects the advertising market depth of each geography.
| Region | Approx. Annual ARPU (2025) | DAP (Daily Active People, approx.) | 
|---|---|---|
| US & Canada | ~$230–250 | ~260 million | 
| Europe | ~$70–80 | ~340 million | 
| Asia-Pacific | ~$20–25 | ~1.4 billion | 
| Rest of World | ~$12–16 | ~1.1 billion | 
The ~15–20x ARPU gap between the US/Canada and the Rest of World cohort reflects several compounding factors:
- Advertiser competition: US digital ad markets are the most liquid in the world. A typical US-facing auction for a 25–34 female consumer has dozens of competing bids from e-commerce, financial services, CPG, and DTC brands.
- Payment infrastructure: The ability to close a transaction after clicking an ad — and therefore for advertisers to attribute ROI — is far stronger in markets with dense credit card penetration.
- GDP per capita and purchasing power: Simply, consumer spend potential in markets Meta can target matters to advertisers.
- Ad format maturity: Video and Stories formats that command premium CPMs are more adopted in developed markets.
The implication is structural: Meta's user growth is increasingly occurring in low-ARPU markets (India, Indonesia, Africa, Latin America) while its monetization leverage sits almost entirely in North America and Western Europe. Growing DAP by 5% in Asia-Pacific is not economically equivalent to growing it 1% in the US.
Gross Margins and Operating Leverage
Meta's Family of Apps segment runs at approximately 55–60% operating margins — one of the highest in large-cap tech, comparable only to Google's Search business. This margin reflects:
- Near-zero marginal cost of serving an additional ad impression
- Fixed cost structure in data centers, which benefit from massive scale
- R&D and headcount, which were rationalized significantly during the 2022–2023 "Year of Efficiency"
Reality Labs, by contrast, drags consolidated operating margins by roughly 8–10 percentage points. Strip out Reality Labs losses, and Meta's core business operates at close to 65–68% margins.
Advertiser Economics
Meta does not disclose CAC metrics at the advertiser level, but third-party data suggests:
- Average CPM on Facebook/Instagram in the US runs approximately $8–15 for broad audiences, with high-intent verticals (financial services, insurance, legal) regularly clearing $25–40 CPM.
- Return on ad spend (ROAS) for direct-response advertisers — the core buyer — typically needs to exceed 2–3x for campaign continuation.
- Meta's Advantage+ AI-driven campaign tool has demonstrably improved ROAS for SMB advertisers, which is the strategic reason Meta has pushed it aggressively; better advertiser ROI increases willingness to raise bids.
Why the Model Is Durable (or Isn't)
Durability Arguments
- 
Network effects are non-linear. Facebook with 3 billion users is not marginally better than Facebook with 2 billion — it is categorically more useful because the probability that any given social connection is on the platform approaches certainty.
- 
The ad tech stack is deeply embedded. Meta's Pixel, Conversions API, and attribution infrastructure are woven into hundreds of thousands of e-commerce and DTC businesses. Switching costs are real.
- 
Reels proved adaptation is possible. When TikTok emerged as a structural threat, Meta pivoted aggressively to short-form video. Reels now has strong engagement metrics and is monetizing at improving (though still below Feed) CPMs. The 2022 panic about TikTok eating Meta's lunch has materially faded.
- 
SMB flywheel. Meta has approximately 10 million active advertisers, the vast majority being small and medium businesses. These businesses have limited alternatives with comparable reach and targeting granularity. Google Search catches intent; Meta creates it.
Durability Risks
- 
iOS 14.5 hangover. Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) framework destroyed a meaningful portion of Meta's attribution capability in 2021-22. Meta has rebuilt much of this through on-platform conversion signals and modeled conversions, but the business is more reliant on probabilistic attribution than it was. Any further platform restriction could re-open that wound.
- 
Attention is zero-sum. Time spent on Meta properties faces competition from YouTube, TikTok, Netflix, and dozens of other applications. Engagement per user, particularly among Gen Z, is contested.
- 
Regulatory overhang. The FTC's attempted breakup of Meta (seeking divestiture of Instagram and WhatsApp) remains an active legal risk. The probability of forced divestiture is low but non-zero, and the distraction cost is real.
Comparison to Closest Competitors
| Metric | Meta | Alphabet (Google) | Snap |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025 Ad Revenue (approx.) | ~$165B | ~$220B | ~$5.5B | ~$4B | 
| DAU/DAP | 3.35B | N/A (Search) | ~450M | ~570M MAU | 
| Operating Margin | ~40–45% | ~32–35% | Breakeven | ~15–20% | 
| Primary Ad Format | Social/Video | Search/YouTube | Social/Video | Visual/Shopping | 
| Advertiser Diversification | High (10M+) | High | Moderate | Moderate | 
Meta's structural advantage over Snap and Pinterest is scale — both in user base and in advertiser competition depth. More advertisers competing for the same slot = higher clearing prices, independent of any product improvement.
Versus Google, the distinction is intent vs. discovery. Google Search monetizes existing demand (someone searching "buy running shoes"). Meta creates latent demand — someone not actively shopping for shoes sees an ad and converts. These are genuinely complementary, which is why most sophisticated advertisers run both. The risk is that Meta becomes more dependent on upper-funnel brand spending if lower-funnel attribution capabilities erode further.
What the Model Looks Like at Scale
Meta is arguably the first advertising business in history to run at true planetary scale — 3.35 billion people engaging daily with its properties. The implications for the model at this scale:
- Incremental user additions have diminishing ARPU impact absent market development in high-income geographies. The next 500 million users are almost certainly lower-ARPU than the current base.
- The growth lever is price, not volume. Meta's revenue growth in 2024-25 was driven primarily by CPM inflation (more advertiser demand, better AI targeting raising conversion rates) rather than net new user additions.
- AI infrastructure investment (~$40–60B in capex guided for 2025–2026) is the primary cost driver. Meta is betting that training frontier AI models and deploying them across ad ranking, content recommendation, and Advantage+ campaigns compounds its targeting advantage. Llama (open-source) is both a research asset and a strategic move to commoditize foundation model infrastructure to reduce dependence on OpenAI/Google.
- WhatsApp monetization remains the clearest undermonetized asset at scale. With 2+ billion users and near-zero current monetization outside the Business API, even modest progress (click-to-WhatsApp ads, payments integration) represents a multi-billion dollar incremental revenue opportunity.
Red Flags and Risk Factors
- 
Reality Labs capital destruction. At $17–19B annual losses with no clear path to profitability before the late 2020s at best, Reality Labs is functionally a research and moonshot division being funded by an advertising business. Zuckerberg's control structure (supervoting shares) means shareholders cannot compel strategic reorientation. This is the defining governance risk.
- 
Concentration in Meta's own surfaces. Unlike Google, which has Display Network and third-party publisher relationships, Meta's ad business is almost entirely dependent on attention generated within its own apps. If a platform-level shift occurs (e.g., AI-native interfaces reducing time on social apps), Meta has fewer hedges.
- 
Regulatory fragmentation. The EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) designates Meta as a "gatekeeper," requiring interoperability with messaging competitors and restricting certain data practices. This adds compliance cost and potentially limits targeting capabilities in Meta's second-largest market.
- 
AI disruption of the ad market itself. If AI assistants (from OpenAI, Google, Apple) become the primary discovery surface for products and services, the "intent creation" model Meta relies on could face structural displacement. This is a 5–10 year risk, not a 12-month risk, but it is real.
- 
Teen engagement and regulatory pressure on youth. Multiple US states have enacted or are advancing legislation restricting teen access to social media. This is primarily a political and reputational risk at present, but could become a usage constraint.
Takeaways for Investors
- 
The core business is genuinely exceptional. At 55–60% operating margins, 10M+ active advertisers, and a self-reinforcing data/targeting flywheel, the Family of Apps is one of the most defensible cash-generating businesses ever built. This deserves a premium multiple.
- 
ARPU expansion, not user growth, is the financial story. Investors should track CPM trends, advertiser count, and average spend per advertiser more closely than daily active people. The latter is a lagging metric.
- 
Reality Labs is the $50B+ question. The Ray-Ban Meta glasses are a proof point that wearable AI interfaces can achieve mass adoption at consumer price points. If smart glasses become a meaningful computing platform by 2028–2030, the option value embedded in Reality Labs becomes enormous. If they don't, Meta will have spent roughly $100B to learn that lesson. The market is currently pricing Reality Labs losses as a tax on an otherwise excellent business — which is approximately correct.
- 
WhatsApp is the unpriced asset. The business-to-consumer messaging and commerce opportunity in Brazil, India, and Indonesia is structurally undervalued relative to what even modest monetization progress would imply at 2 billion users.
- 
Watch capex discipline. Meta's willingness to guide $40–60B in annual capex for AI infrastructure is either the most rational investment in tech today or a repetition of the 2021 metaverse overinvestment. The difference — and it matters enormously — is that AI compute is general-purpose infrastructure benefiting the ad business today, not a speculative consumer platform. That distinction deserves weight.
Bottom line: Meta is a structurally advantaged advertising oligopolist funding a high-conviction long-duration bet at massive cost. For investors with appropriate time horizons, the question is not whether the core business is good — it clearly is — but whether Zuckerberg's vision of the next computing platform justifies the capital allocation risk. History suggests betting against his product instincts has been expensive. History also suggests that no technology platform cycle lasts forever.
This article reflects analysis based on publicly available information through early 2026. All financial figures are approximations derived from public filings and should not be taken as audited data.
