title: Goldman Sachs sees Brent at $80 in 2027: What it means for India's oil import bill
snippet: Goldman Sachs sees Brent at $80 in 2027, offering India import-bill relief if Mideast supplies recover; see what could change.
content:
Goldman Sachs expects global crude oil prices to moderate in 2027 as oil supplies from the Middle East gradually recover, potentially giving relief to major oil-importing countries such as India. The investment bank, however, warned that a new escalation of the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran could keep prices elevated longer than anticipated.
In a report published in October, Goldman Sachs Research said benchmark Brent crude oil could average $80 a barrel in 2027. The bank also raised its forecast for December 2026 to $90 a barrel from its earlier estimate of $85.
For India, which relies heavily on imported crude oil to meet domestic demand, a sustained decline in international prices could help contain the oil import bill, ease pressure on the current account deficit and moderate inflationary pressures. The extent of the relief will depend on the pace of supply recovery, developments in the Middle East and the rupee’s movement against the US dollar.
Why does Goldman Sachs expect oil prices to fall in 2027?
Goldman Sachs expects the global oil market to move towards a surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026 and remain in surplus through 2027. The bank sees this change in the balance between supply and demand as a key reason for its forecast of lower crude oil prices.
Oil supplies from the Persian Gulf fell sharply after the conflict broke out. Exporters have since adapted to the disruption faster than expected, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
The bank estimates that Persian Gulf oil exports had recovered to around their 2025 average by late September. This estimate includes approximately four million barrels per day of so-called dark exports, referring to shipments carried by tankers that switch off their tracking transponders to conceal their movements.
Goldman Sachs also expects exports to increase further as producers adapt to the disruption and expand transportation capacity, particularly through pipelines and a larger tanker fleet.
The improvement in supply has coincided with weaker oil demand. According to Goldman Sachs Research, global oil demand in September 2026 was around 1.3 million barrels per day below the 2025 average as higher prices weighed on consumption.
The combination of higher production outside the Persian Gulf and lower demand helped bring the market much closer to balance. Goldman Sachs estimated that demand exceeded supply by only 300,000 barrels per day in September, compared with a supply deficit of 7.2 million barrels per day in March.
Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research and head of oil research at Goldman Sachs, stated the expected return to a surplus as “the key driver” of the bank’s forecast for crude prices to moderate.
Why could crude oil remain expensive despite the supply recovery?
The projected decline in oil prices is not guaranteed. Goldman Sachs has cautioned that renewed escalation in the Middle East remains a significant upside risk.
The report noted that dated Brent crude scheduled for delivery in the following month was trading above $130 a barrel, benchmark Brent futures had recently moved above $100.
The difference shows the pressure in the physical oil market, where buyers are willing to pay elevated prices for immediate supplies amid concerns about disruptions and depleted inventories.
“Physical prices remain elevated because escalation threatens supply while near-record-low global inventories fuel strong restocking demand,” Struyven wrote.
Goldman Sachs estimated that spot Brent prices included a risk premium of nearly $23 a barrel above their fair value because renewed escalation could restrict supplies and further deplete inventories.
Oil infrastructure remains vulnerable to attacks. Iran or Yemen’s Houthi rebels could target ports, pipelines and oil fields, potentially disrupting production and exports across the region.
The conflict’s impact on the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy shipments, has also affected oil consumption. Goldman Sachs Research estimated that global oil demand in the third quarter of 2026 was down 3.3 million barrels per day from a year earlier, with much of the weakness concentrated in China, the Middle East and developed Asian economies.
The bank expects much of this lost demand to recover as the availability and affordability of refined petroleum products improve. However, it estimates that oil demand could still be 700,000 barrels per day below its hypothetical path without the conflict by the fourth quarter of 2027, partly because the disruption has accelerated the use of electric vehicles and trucks in China.
This creates two competing forces for prices. A recovery in Middle Eastern supplies could push prices lower, while renewed attacks, shipping disruptions or a faster-than-expected recovery in demand could limit the decline.
India is particularly exposed to changes in global crude oil prices because it relies heavily on imported supplies to meet domestic demand.
According to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), India’s crude oil import dependence stood at approximately 88.7% in the financial year 2025-26. The country imported around 246.6 million tonnes of crude oil that year, with the import bill estimated at about $126 billion.
What does an $80 Brent crude forecast mean for India’s oil import bill?
A sustained decline in international crude prices could reduce the amount India spends on importing oil, provided import volumes and other costs remain broadly unchanged.
The potential impact is significant. India imports roughly 1.8 billion to 2 billion barrels of crude oil annually. Every $1 per barrel change in crude prices can alter the annual oil import bill by approximately $1.8 billion to $2 billion, depending on import volumes.
At an average Brent price of $80 a barrel in 2027, India could benefit from lower international benchmark prices than it would under a prolonged high-price scenario. However, Goldman Sachs’ forecast should not be interpreted as a direct estimate of India’s oil import bill.
Brent is an international benchmark, whereas the price India pays depends on the composition of its crude imports, the discounts or premiums on individual grades, freight and insurance costs, the rupee-dollar exchange rate and the volume of oil purchased.
The forecast also refers to the calendar year 2027, India’s government accounts are organised by financial year, from April to March. The impact on the import bill for 2027-28 would depend on prices across the entire financial year, not just the average Brent price for the calendar year.
How could lower oil prices affect inflation and the rupee?
A decline in crude oil prices could ease pressure on India’s economy through several channels. First, lower import costs could improve India’s trade balance by reducing the value of crude oil purchased from overseas. A smaller oil import bill, all else being equal, could also help contain the current account deficit, which measures the gap between the country’s external receipts and payments.
Second, cheaper crude could reduce input costs for sectors that depend heavily on petroleum products, including transport, aviation, logistics and manufacturing. Lower fuel and freight costs could help moderate inflation, although the extent of the benefit would depend on how much of the reduction is passed on to consumers.
Third, lower demand for dollars to pay for oil imports could ease pressure on the rupee. The currency’s movement, however, also depends on capital flows, interest rates and other external factors.
The reverse is also true. Higher crude prices increase the cost of imports and can put pressure on the rupee, inflation and the country’s external balances. As reported by The ndian Express in its July 2026 report every $1-per-barrel increase in crude prices could add up to $2 billion to India’s annual oil import bill, based on the country’s import volumes.
The benefits for consumers may not be immediate. Retail petrol and diesel prices also depend on domestic taxes, refining and distribution costs, and the pricing decisions of oil marketing companies. A decline in Brent crude therefore does not automatically translate into an equivalent reduction in fuel prices at petrol pumps.
What are the risks to India’s oil import outlook?
The main risk is that the expected recovery in Middle Eastern supplies fails to materialise or is interrupted by fresh attacks and shipping disruptions.
Goldman Sachs’ forecast assumes that producers will continue adapting to the conflict and that global oil supply will eventually exceed demand. A prolonged disruption to exports or transportation routes could delay this adjustment and keep crude prices above the bank’s projected average.
The report also focuses on the role of global inventories. Low inventories can amplify price movements when traders and refiners attempt to secure supplies. Even if exports recover, the process of rebuilding stocks could sustain demand and keep physical oil prices elevated.
India’s actual import costs will also depend on the price of the crude grades it buys, shipping expenses and currency movements. A weaker rupee could offset some of the savings from lower dollar-denominated crude prices. Changes in import volumes would further influence the final bill.
Goldman Sachs’ forecast of Brent crude averaging $80 a barrel in 2027 points to the possibility of some relief for India after a period of severe volatility in energy markets. A sustained decline could lower the country’s oil import costs, improve its external balances and ease inflationary pressures.
The outlook remains conditional, however. The bank expects supplies to recover and the global market to move into surplus, but it also warns that renewed escalation in the Middle East could push prices higher.
The key question for India is not simply whether Brent crude reaches $80 a barrel. The more important factors will be the average price of the crude it imports, the duration of the price decline, the rupee’s performance and the extent to which lower global prices translate into savings for the economy.
A sustained fall in prices would provide meaningful relief to one of India’s largest import expenses. A temporary dip, followed by renewed supply disruptions, would offer far less comfort.

title: D-Street Outlook: 5 Key Factors Including India, US CPI Inflation Data And Crude Oil Prices To Drive Markets Next Week - Outlook Money
snippet: Stock market outlook for next week: key drivers include US and India CPI inflation, crude oil prices, FII flows, and a ...
content:
Summary of this article
- Indian stock markets will observe a holiday on Monday.
- Retail inflation numbers from India and US face scrutiny.
- Crude oil price swings and institutional fund flows dictate trends.
Domestic stock market indices finished the session in the green on November 6, 2026, with the Nifty 50 closing at 25,030.35 up by 493.75 points or 2.01 per cent and the Sensex closing at 81,028.02, up by 1,718.01 points or 2.17 per cent.
The optimism seen in the market was led by a shift in global sentiment and sustained buying interest from foreign institutional investors. As D-Street readies itself for the new week, investors are set to monitor factors such as a truncated trading week, India and United States CPI inflation data for October, crude oil prices, and the pattern of institutional investments.
Truncated Trading Week
The upcoming week will see fewer than normal trading sessions as the Indian stock market will remain closed on Monday, November 9 on Bali Pratipada. This in turn shortens the window for market participants to react to developments and global cues that emerge while domestic exchanges are shut. A tighter trading schedule can potentially impact D-Street activity by leading to higher volatility and concentrated trading volumes as investors rush to adjust their portfolios in fewer than the normal number of trading sessions.
India CPI Inflation Data
Domestic investors will continue to monitor India's retail inflation data for the month of October 2026. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is set to release the data on November 12. The central bank monitors inflation to shape its monetary policy and decide on the future trajectory of interest rates. A higher-than-expected domestic inflation figure can potentially impact D-Street activity by dampening hopes of near-term rate cuts, weighing down rate-sensitive sectors like banking, auto, and real estate.
US Consumer Price Index (CPI) Inflation (October)
The trajectory of prices in the world's largest economy remains a key factor for investors. The October CPI data from the United States is expected to provide investors a clearer picture of whether inflation is cooling fast enough to warrant further rate reductions by the US Federal Reserve. Any negative markers in this inflation data can impact D-Street activity by sparking a global risk-off sentiment and triggering foreign fund outflows from Indian equities.
Crude Oil Prices
The movement of crude oil prices remains a key factor for India's economic outlook, given the country's reliance on energy imports. Crude oil markets continue to be closely watched, with Brent Crude futures currently trading at $98.32 and WTI Crude futures at $90.83 as of November 7, 2026. A drop in energy costs can boost D-Street activity by improving corporate margins across manufacturing sectors and lifting the overall market mood.
Institutional Inflows
Market sentiment will continue to be influenced by the behaviour of Foreign Institutional Investors and Domestic Institutional Investors. The gains seen in the market this week were supported by consistent purchases from foreign funds, with FIIs recording a net purchase of Rs 45,960.02 crore in the cash segment in November 2026, a sharp reversal from their net sale of Rs 45,161.71 crore in October 2026.
Conversely, Domestic Institutional Investors have logged a net sale of Rs 24,196.52 crore in November, shifting from a robust net purchase of Rs 62,220.11 crore during the previous month. A reversal in these institutional buying patterns can potentially impact D-Street activity by removing market support and initiating a correction in benchmark indices.

title: Crude oil price fall offers India relief, but exporters await cheaper inputs: IIFT Vice Chancellor K Rangarajan- Moneycontrol.com
snippet: Brent crude has fallen sharply from its October 30 peak of $118 a barrel to around $92 on November 10, amid hopes of de-escalation in the US-Iran conflict.
content:
The sharp correction in crude oil prices could ease India’s import bill and inflationary pressures while improving the competitiveness of non-oil exports, but the benefits will depend on whether lower prices sustain and translate into cheaper industrial inputs and shipping costs, said K. Rangarajan, Vice Chancellor of the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT).
Brent crude has fallen sharply from its October 30 peak of $118 a barrel to around $92 on November 10, amid hopes of de-escalation in the US-Iran conflict. The decline offers some relief to India, which imports a large share of its crude requirements and faced a sharp rise in energy costs in recent months.
"Oil going down from $100 is good," Rangarajan said, adding that lower oil prices would help non-oil exports by reducing the cost of production and exports.
However, easing crude prices does not immediately remove risks to India's external sector. Disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a significant share of India's crude imports traditionally passes, continue to leave energy supplies vulnerable to geopolitical developments.
The correction could also help narrow India's trade deficit, which has widened despite strong export growth. Merchandise exports rose 18.5 percent to $259.9 billion in the first half of FY27. However, the second half could be more challenging as the high base, weaker European demand and uncertainty over US tariffs weigh on shipments.
"The second half will be harder: the base is higher, oil-price gains will fade, European demand is weak, and US duties remain," he said.
The fall in international crude prices has already begun reflecting in India's import costs. The Indian crude basket fell to $94.5 a barrel on November 5, its lowest level in two months, declining 20% in a week from $118.7 on October 30.
Relief for current account, inflation
Rangarajan said every sustained $10-a-barrel increase in crude prices adds around $13-15 billion to India's net import bill. It also adds 0.3-0.4 percentage points to the current account deficit (CAD) as a share of gross domestic product (GDP), increases consumer price inflation by 25-30 basis points with partial pass-through, and reduces economic growth by 15-20 basis points, according to his estimates.
The recent correction, if sustained, could therefore ease pressure on India's external balances and inflation. However, the extent of the improvement will depend on the average price of crude imported over the coming months, rather than movements in international futures alone.
The geopolitical risk has also not disappeared. Although oil prices fell for a second consecutive session on November 10 after US President Donald Trump indicated restraint on further military action against Iran, the US naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz remained in place and attacks on shipping continued.
Lower oil may not immediately ease exporters' costs
For India’s export sector, cheaper crude could benefit more than just lower energy costs. Petrochemicals, plastics, textiles, fertilisers, paints, packaging and transport are among the industries exposed to fluctuations in oil and gas prices.
Rangarajan said higher naphtha prices feed into polymer costs, which account for 60-70% of the expenses of plastic processors. Similarly, higher prices of purified terephthalic acid (PTA) and monoethylene glycol (MEG), used in polyester production, affect synthetic-fibre textile manufacturers.
Fertiliser manufacturers also face higher costs when liquefied natural gas (LNG), ammonia and diammonium phosphate (DAP) become expensive, increasing the government's subsidy burden.
Diesel and freight costs are another concern, particularly for smaller exporters operating on fixed-price overseas contracts. Higher logistics costs can erode margins when exporters cannot pass them on to buyers.
Rangarajan said the cost burden so far has largely been borne by oil marketing companies and the government, while industrial users have faced market prices for bulk diesel, naphtha, furnace oil, LNG and aviation turbine fuel.
"Competitiveness is hurt mainly through industrial input costs, not retail fuel," he said.
He suggested that small exporters explore price-escalation clauses in contracts, Export Credit Guarantee Corporation cover and support available under the Niryat Protsahan component of the government's Export Promotion Mission.
India needs to diversify energy supplies
The recent volatility has also underscored India's dependence on vulnerable shipping routes and the need to diversify crude and gas supplies.
Rangarajan said India should expand its strategic petroleum reserves, secure longer-term crude supply contracts with countries such as the US, Guyana, Brazil and West African producers, and invest in overseas oil assets through ONGC Videsh.
He said India should also accelerate electric vehicle adoption, shift more freight to rail and coastal shipping, and diversify LNG supplies, given that Qatari gas shipments also pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
Exports could reach $1 tn
Despite the global uncertainty, Rangarajan expects India's merchandise exports to reach $480-500 billion in FY27. Combined goods and services exports could approach $950 billion, though he expects the $1 trillion milestone to be reached in 2027. India's total exports of merchandise and services reached an estimated $476.20 billion during the April–September 2026–27 period, marking a 13.84 percent growth compared to the same period in the previous year.
He said India's positioning as a trusted alternative to China and other emerging markets needs to be strengthened through greater participation by Indian businesses in international markets, rather than relying only on government messaging.
On trade diversification, he said the agreements with the UK and the European Union could partly offset losses in the US market over three to five years, particularly for textiles, leather, footwear, marine products and gems and jewellery.
However, he cautioned that the US remains a critical market for Indian exporters and a trade agreement with Washington continues to matter.

title: Brent Crude Volatility: India's Economic Fault Line & Stock Winners/Losers
snippet: Sep 23, 2026 · Unpack Brent crude volatility's ripple effect on India's import bill, inflation, and key stocks like RIL, ONGC, IOC, and IndiGo. Get our expert investor playbook.
content:
Key Takeaway
Brent crude's unpredictable swings, fueled by US-Iran dynamics, are a critical determinant for India's economic stability. Investors must navigate this volatility by strategically positioning in OMCs and aviation during price dips, while exercising caution with E&P and energy-intensive manufacturing.
India's economy is acutely sensitive to Brent crude price fluctuations, with recent US-Iran geopolitical maneuvers injecting fresh uncertainty. Our deep dive reveals how these price shifts directly impact India's inflation, current account, and the profitability of key sectors from oil marketing to aviation. Understand the specific stocks poised to win or lose and develop an actionable investment strategy.
Brent Crude's Geopolitical Tightrope: Unpacking India's Economic Vulnerability
The global oil market finds itself in a familiar, yet perpetually precarious, dance with geopolitics. Recent overtures towards a potential US-Iran nuclear deal resolution have sent ripples through Brent crude futures, creating a volatile environment that directly impacts highly import-dependent economies like India. This isn't just about the price at the pump; it's a fundamental economic tremor, influencing everything from the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) monetary policy stance to the bottom lines of India's largest corporations and the daily spending power of its 1.4 billion citizens.
For India, the stakes couldn't be higher. As the world's third-largest oil importer, purchasing over 85% of its crude requirements from international markets, every dollar movement in Brent crude translates into billions on its import bill. A sustained $10 increase in crude prices can expand India's current account deficit (CAD) by approximately 0.5% of GDP and add around 25-30 basis points to headline inflation. This immediate and profound impact underscores why the current Brent crude volatility, driven by the unpredictable pendulum of US-Iran relations, is not merely a market headline but a critical economic fault line for the Indian subcontinent. The added layer of a strengthening US dollar further exacerbates this challenge, making dollar-denominated crude purchases even more expensive in rupee terms.
How Brent Crude Swings Impact the Indian Stock Market: A Sector-by-Sector Breakdown
The direct correlation between Brent crude prices and India's macroeconomic indicators ensures a significant, albeit nuanced, impact on the Indian stock market. Historically, periods of sustained crude price increases have often coincided with inflationary pressures and rupee depreciation, leading to broader market corrections. Conversely, a benign crude environment typically provides a tailwind for equities, especially sectors with high energy intensity.
Who Wins and Who Loses from Brent Crude Volatility in India?
The impact of crude price fluctuations is not uniform across sectors. A detailed understanding of these differential effects is crucial for savvy investors:
- Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) – Potential Winners (if crude falls): Companies like Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL), and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL) benefit significantly from falling crude prices. Lower crude acquisition costs, coupled with a lag in adjusting retail fuel prices (especially during periods of stable government intervention), can expand their marketing margins. Conversely, rising crude prices can squeeze their profitability, as they often absorb a portion of the price hike before passing it on to consumers.
- Aviation Sector – Strong Winners (if crude falls): Fuel typically constitutes 30-40% of an airline's operating costs. Therefore, a decline in crude prices directly translates into lower Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) costs, boosting profit margins for carriers like InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) and SpiceJet. The last significant crude price drop in 2020 saw a sharp rebound in airline stock prices, as investors priced in improved profitability.
- Logistics Sector – Winners (if crude falls): Companies involved in road and sea freight, where fuel is a major operational expense, see their costs decrease with falling crude prices. This can improve their operating leverage and profitability, benefiting players across the supply chain.
- Oil Exploration & Production (E&P) Companies – Losers (if crude falls significantly): Companies like ONGC and Oil India are direct beneficiaries of higher crude prices, as their revenue is directly linked to global benchmarks. A significant decline in Brent crude can erode their profitability and valuation, as their upstream earnings diminish. For instance, ONGC's consolidated net profit often correlates strongly with the average crude price realization.
- Manufacturing Companies (High Energy Input) – Losers (if crude rises): Sectors such as cement, steel, chemicals, and fertilizers have substantial energy input costs. Rising crude prices translate into higher manufacturing expenses, impacting their margins and pricing power. Companies in these sectors may struggle to pass on the full cost increase to consumers, leading to reduced profitability.
- Chemicals Sector – Losers (if crude rises): The chemicals industry relies heavily on crude oil derivatives as feedstocks. An increase in crude prices directly inflates raw material costs, compressing margins for chemical manufacturers.
Stock-by-Stock Breakdown: Navigating the Oil Price Tides
Understanding the specific exposure of individual companies is paramount for informed investment decisions during periods of Brent crude volatility.
- Reliance Industries (RIL): As a diversified conglomerate with significant interests in refining & petrochemicals (Oil-to-Chemicals or O2C segment) and oil & gas E&P, RIL has a complex relationship with crude prices. While higher crude prices boost its E&P segment (though relatively smaller), they can also impact its O2C margins, especially if product cracks don't keep pace. However, RIL's growing digital (Jio) and retail segments offer diversification, making it less solely dependent on crude than pure-play energy firms. Its current market capitalization exceeding ₹18 lakh crore (approx. $215 billion) reflects its diversified strength.
- ONGC (Oil and Natural Gas Corporation): A quintessential E&P play, ONGC's fortunes are directly tied to crude oil prices. A $10/barrel change in Brent crude can significantly impact its revenue and net profit. Currently trading around a P/E multiple lower than its historical average, its valuation often reflects market expectations of future crude price trends. Investors should monitor its daily production figures and government policies on windfall taxes, which can further impact its profitability.
- Oil India Ltd.: Similar to ONGC, Oil India is an upstream E&P company. Its profitability is highly sensitive to crude prices. A sustained downturn in Brent crude would negatively impact its earnings, while an upturn would provide a strong tailwind. Its smaller size relative to ONGC makes it potentially more volatile to crude price swings.
- Indian Oil Corporation (IOC): As India's largest OMC, IOC benefits from lower crude prices due to improved marketing margins. Conversely, sharp spikes in crude can erode its profitability if retail price increases are delayed. Its significant refining capacity also means inventory gains/losses can play a role. A strong balance sheet and government backing provide some stability, but its stock performance is highly correlated with the crude price cycle.
- Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) & Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL): These OMCs share similar dynamics with IOC. Their profitability is inversely related to crude prices, assuming stable retail pricing. Government policy on fuel subsidies and price deregulation is a key factor to watch. When crude prices fell sharply in 2020, these stocks saw significant buying interest due to margin expansion expectations.
- InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo): As India's largest airline, IndiGo is a direct beneficiary of falling crude prices. A 10% reduction in ATF prices can significantly boost its operating margins. Conversely, a sustained increase in Brent crude can severely pressure its profitability, as seen in periods like mid-2022 when crude prices soared past $100/barrel. Its current market cap of over ₹1 lakh crore (approx. $12 billion) makes it a bellwether for the aviation sector's health.
Expert Perspective: Bulls vs. Bears on Brent and India
The current environment fosters a divergence of expert opinions on both crude trajectory and India's resilience.
The Bulls argue: "While US-Iran talks introduce near-term volatility, the broader demand-supply fundamentals for crude remain robust. Global economic recovery, particularly from China, will underpin demand. Any sustained dip in Brent below $75/barrel is likely to be short-lived, presenting a buying opportunity for E&P companies like ONGC and Oil India, which are currently trading at attractive valuations relative to their long-term earning potential. Furthermore, India's economic growth momentum provides a buffer against moderate crude price shocks, allowing OMCs to eventually pass on costs. Diversified giants like RIL, with their expanding consumer-facing businesses, offer insulation from pure-play energy price risks."
The Bears counter: "The US-Iran situation is a significant downside risk for crude, potentially unleashing more supply into an already uncertain demand landscape. Persistent inflation, globally and domestically, could force central banks to maintain hawkish stances, slowing economic growth and consequently, oil demand. For India, a sustained period of high crude prices (above $90/barrel) combined with a strong dollar would be a 'perfect storm,' severely impacting the current account, fueling inflation, and prompting aggressive RBI intervention. This would inevitably lead to broad-based market corrections, with OMCs and aviation stocks facing significant headwinds due to margin compression and demand elasticity. Even diversified plays like RIL would feel the pinch in their energy segments, and their consumer businesses might face weakened demand due to inflationary pressures."
Actionable Investor Playbook: Navigating the Volatility
For investors seeking to capitalize on or mitigate the risks associated with Brent crude volatility, a multi-pronged strategy is essential:
- Buy Strategy (on Crude Dips):
        
  - OMCs (IOC, BPCL, HPCL): Consider accumulating these stocks on significant crude price declines (e.g., Brent sustained below $75/barrel). This typically signals expanding marketing margins and improved profitability. Look for entry points when their P/E ratios are below historical averages. Time horizon: Medium-term (6-12 months) to capture the full margin cycle.
  - Aviation (IndiGo, SpiceJet): These are high-beta plays on falling crude. Sharp drops in Brent (e.g., $5-$10/barrel within a week) present strong buying opportunities. Monitor ATF price trends closely. Time horizon: Short to medium-term (3-9 months) for cyclical gains.
  - Logistics: Companies with high fuel costs in their operational structure could see improved margins. Research specific companies with strong market positioning.
- Sell/Reduce Exposure Strategy (on Crude Rises):
        
  - E&P Companies (ONGC, Oil India): While higher crude benefits them, consider trimming positions if you anticipate a prolonged downturn or if geopolitical resolutions point to increased supply. Their valuations often peak with crude price peaks. Time horizon: Tactical, based on crude outlook.
  - Energy-Intensive Manufacturing & Chemicals: If crude prices show sustained upward momentum (e.g., Brent above $90/barrel for several weeks), consider reducing exposure to these sectors as their input costs will rise, squeezing margins.
- Watch Strategy:
        
  - Reliance Industries (RIL): Given its diversification, RIL acts as a partial hedge. Monitor its O2C segment's Gross Refining Margins (GRMs) and petrochemical cracks, alongside the performance of Jio and Retail. It's a 'watch' for overall market sentiment and as a barometer for broader economic health rather than a direct crude play.
  - RBI Policy: The central bank's stance on interest rates will be heavily influenced by crude-driven inflation. Hawkish signals could depress broader market sentiment.
Risk Matrix: Assessing the Unpredictable
Investing in crude-sensitive sectors carries inherent risks, primarily driven by the unpredictable nature of global events. Here's a breakdown:
- Geopolitical Escalation (High Probability, High Impact): A sudden deterioration in US-Iran relations or other major geopolitical flashpoints (e.g., Middle East conflicts, Russia-Ukraine war developments) could cause immediate and sharp spikes in crude prices. This is the 'black swan' event that can quickly invalidate investment theses. Probability: High. Impact: High.
- Stronger US Dollar (Medium Probability, Medium Impact): Persistent strength in the US dollar against the rupee makes crude imports more expensive for India, even if dollar-denominated crude prices remain stable. This can erode the benefits of moderate crude prices or exacerbate the pain of rising crude. Probability: Medium. Impact: Medium.
- Global Economic Slowdown (Medium Probability, Medium Impact): A significant slowdown in global economic growth, potentially triggered by aggressive central bank tightening, could depress oil demand. While this might lower crude prices (benefiting OMCs/Aviation), it would also signal broader economic distress, potentially impacting overall market sentiment and corporate earnings across sectors. Probability: Medium. Impact: Medium.
- Domestic Policy Intervention (Medium Probability, Low-Medium Impact): Government intervention in fuel pricing (e.g., excise duty changes, subsidies) can alter the profitability landscape for OMCs, irrespective of crude prices. While less impactful than global events, it introduces a layer of regulatory risk. Probability: Medium. Impact: Low-Medium.
What to Watch Next: Catalysts for Crude and Indian Markets
Investors should closely monitor several key indicators and events that will shape the narrative around Brent crude and its impact on Indian stocks:
- US-Iran Nuclear Deal Negotiations: Any official statements, leaks, or developments regarding a potential resolution will be critical. A breakthrough could increase Iranian oil supply, pushing crude prices down.
- OPEC+ Meetings and Production Decisions: The cartel's monthly meetings and decisions on production quotas can significantly influence global supply and price. The next major meeting dates should be marked on calendars.
- Weekly EIA and API Crude Inventory Reports (USA): These reports provide insights into US oil demand and supply dynamics, often causing short-term price movements.
- RBI Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) Meetings: The RBI's stance on interest rates, heavily influenced by inflation (where crude plays a major role), will impact liquidity and broader market sentiment.
- India's Merchandise Trade Data & CAD Figures: Monthly trade data, especially oil import figures, and quarterly Current Account Deficit releases will offer concrete evidence of crude's impact on India's external balances.
- Global Economic Data (PMI, Inflation, GDP): Macroeconomic indicators from major economies (US, China, Europe) will signal global demand trends for oil.
The dance between geopolitics, supply-demand fundamentals, and India's economic resilience will continue to define the trajectory of Brent crude and its profound implications for the Indian stock market. Astute investors will remain vigilant, adapting their strategies to the evolving landscape.

title: Brent Crude Above $90: India's Economy, Stocks Face Inflation Shock
snippet: Aug 17, 2026 · Middle East tensions push Brent crude past $90. Discover how rising oil prices will impact India's economy, current account, RBI policy, and specific NSE/BSE stocks. Deep dive for investors.
content:
Key Takeaway
Escalating Middle East tensions pushing Brent crude above $90/barrel fundamentally alters India's economic calculus, triggering inflation concerns, a wider current account deficit, and potential RBI monetary tightening. Investors must brace for sector-specific volatility, favoring upstream oil and defense while cautioning against airlines and consumer discretionary.
Geopolitical tremors from the Middle East have sent Brent crude soaring past the critical $90/barrel mark, reigniting fears across global markets. For India, a net oil importer, this surge portends significant economic headwinds, from inflationary pressures to a widening current account deficit. Our deep dive dissects the immediate and long-term implications for the Indian stock market, identifying key winners and losers amidst this unfolding energy crisis.
Brent Crude Surges Past $90: Decoding the Geopolitical Oil Shock on India's Economy and Stock Market
The global energy landscape has been abruptly redrawn. For the first time since October 2023, Brent crude oil has breached the psychologically significant $90 per barrel threshold, driven by escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. This isn't merely a headline; it's a fundamental shift that reverberates through the intricate capillaries of the global economy, and nowhere is this impact felt more acutely than in India, a nation heavily reliant on imported energy.
The immediate catalyst for this surge is the heightened risk premium attached to oil supplies from the volatile Middle East region. While specific production cuts haven't been announced, the specter of supply disruptions from a major oil-producing region, coupled with ongoing OPEC+ output restraints, has injected a potent dose of uncertainty into the market. This scenario is far more than a transient fluctuation; it signals a potential prolonged period of elevated energy costs, fundamentally altering the economic outlook for major importers like India.
For India, the 'why now' is critical. As the world's third-largest oil importer, every $10 increase in crude prices typically inflates India's import bill by approximately $15 billion annually. With Brent crude already up significantly from its recent lows, this translates directly into a widening current account deficit (CAD). A larger CAD puts downward pressure on the Indian Rupee (INR), making imports even more expensive and creating a self-reinforcing cycle of inflationary pressure. This confluence of factors makes the current oil spike a paramount concern for policymakers at the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and investors tracking the Indian equity market.
How Will $90 Oil Impact India's Macroeconomic Stability and RBI Policy?
The direct consequences of sustained $90+ Brent crude for India are multifaceted and largely negative. Firstly, inflation, a persistent concern for the RBI, receives a fresh impetus. Higher crude prices translate into increased fuel costs for transportation, manufacturing, and even agriculture, feeding into both wholesale and retail inflation. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), already hovering near the upper end of the RBI's comfort zone, risks breaching it decisively, complicating the central bank's monetary policy stance.
The RBI faces an unenviable dilemma. Should inflation persist or accelerate, the central bank will be compelled to consider tighter monetary policy – meaning higher interest rates – to anchor inflation expectations. This would be a significant pivot from the market's recent anticipation of rate cuts later in the year. Higher interest rates, while combating inflation, inevitably dampen economic growth, increase borrowing costs for corporations, and temper consumer demand, creating a challenging environment for overall economic expansion.
Historically, periods of sustained high oil prices have often coincided with periods of slower economic growth and increased financial market volatility in India. For instance, in 2022, when Brent crude briefly touched $120, the Nifty 50 corrected by nearly 10% from its peak, and corporate earnings growth faced significant margin pressure. While the current situation isn't as extreme, the directional impact remains the same, requiring investors to reassess their portfolio allocations and risk exposures.
Beyond inflation and monetary policy, the widening CAD poses a risk to the Indian Rupee. A depreciating INR makes foreign investments more expensive for Indian companies and can deter foreign portfolio investors (FPIs), leading to capital outflows. The interplay between crude prices, inflation, interest rates, and currency movements forms a complex web that will dictate India's economic trajectory in the coming months.
Which Indian Stocks Will Win and Lose from Sustained High Oil Prices?
The impact of escalating crude prices on the Indian stock market is highly granular, creating distinct winners and losers across sectors. Investors must adopt a nuanced approach, understanding that broad market sentiment may be bearish, but specific pockets can offer defensive plays or even outperform.
The Winners: Upstream Oil & Gas, Defense, and Pricing Power Plays
- Oil and Gas Exploration Companies: This is the most direct beneficiary. Upstream players like Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC, NSE: ONGC) and Oil India Limited (NSE: OIL) see their realizations improve significantly as global crude prices rise. Their revenues and profitability are directly tied to the price of crude oil. ONGC, with a market capitalization exceeding INR 3.4 trillion and a trailing P/E ratio of around 7x, is particularly sensitive to these movements. Higher crude prices directly enhance the value of their oil and gas reserves, potentially leading to re-rating opportunities. Oil India, a smaller but similarly structured player, also benefits proportionally.
- Defence Sector: Geopolitical uncertainty inherently boosts the defense sector globally and in India. Increased perceived threats lead to higher defense spending. Indian defense companies like Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd (HAL, NSE: HAL) and Bharat Dynamics Ltd (NSE: BDL) could see increased order flows as the government prioritizes national security in a more volatile global environment. This is an indirect, but potent, thematic play.
- Companies with Strong Pricing Power in Commodity Sectors: While general inflationary pressures hurt, companies that can effectively pass on increased input costs to consumers due to strong brand equity or market dominance might fare better. This is a more subtle play, requiring deep fundamental analysis of individual companies' competitive advantages.
The Losers: Fuel-Sensitive Sectors and Consumer Discretionary
- Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs): Downstream players like Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL, NSE: HINDPETRO), Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL, NSE: BPCL), and Indian Oil Corporation (IOC, NSE: IOC) face a complex challenge. While they benefit from inventory gains when crude prices rise, their profitability is heavily influenced by the government's ability to allow them to pass on the full cost increase to consumers. If retail fuel prices are kept artificially low for political reasons, OMCs suffer margin compression. HPCL, with a market cap of over INR 70,000 crore, saw its margins squeezed significantly during previous periods of high crude and controlled retail prices.
- City Gas Distribution (CGD) Companies: Companies like Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL, NSE: IGL) and Mahanagar Gas Limited (MGL, NSE: MGL) are also vulnerable. While they primarily deal in natural gas, which has its own price dynamics, higher crude prices often create an upward pull on all energy commodities. Moreover, the government's pricing formula for domestic gas is often linked to international crude benchmarks, impacting their input costs. If they cannot fully pass on these costs to consumers, their margins will erode.
- Airlines: This sector is notoriously sensitive to fuel prices. Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) constitutes 30-40% of an airline's operating costs. A sustained increase in crude prices directly impacts the profitability of carriers like SpiceJet (NSE: SPICEJET) and InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo, NSE: INDIGO). While they can try to hike fares, demand elasticity and intense competition limit this ability, often leading to reduced margins or even losses. IndiGo, despite its market leadership, will face headwinds.
- Logistics and Shipping Companies: Diesel is a primary input for road and sea transport. Higher fuel costs directly increase operational expenses for logistics players, potentially impacting their profitability if they cannot fully pass on these costs to clients. Companies like Container Corporation of India (CONCOR, NSE: CONCOR) and other freight carriers will face margin pressures.
- Petrochemicals and Plastic Manufacturers: Crude oil is a key feedstock for the petrochemical industry. Companies involved in manufacturing plastics, polymers, and other crude derivatives will see their raw material costs escalate. Unless they possess significant pricing power, their margins will be squeezed.
- Automobile Sector: High fuel prices can dampen consumer demand for vehicles, especially those with lower fuel efficiency. Increased transportation costs also impact the entire automotive supply chain. Companies like Tata Motors (NSE: TATAMOTORS) and Maruti Suzuki India (NSE: MARUTI) could experience a slowdown in sales, particularly in the passenger vehicle segment, as disposable incomes are diverted to fuel.
- Consumer Discretionary Goods: As inflation erodes purchasing power, consumers tend to cut back on non-essential spending. Sectors like retail, consumer durables, and leisure could see reduced demand, impacting companies operating in these spaces.
- IT Services: While not directly impacted by fuel costs, a global economic slowdown stemming from higher energy prices and potential monetary tightening in key client geographies (US, Europe) could lead to reduced client spending on IT services, indirectly affecting Indian IT majors like Tata Consultancy Services (TCS, NSE: TCS) and Infosys (NSE: INFY).
Expert Perspectives: Bulls vs. Bears on India's Oil Shock Resilience
The current oil price surge elicits contrasting views among market strategists. The 'bearish' camp argues that India's economy, already grappling with persistent inflation and a challenging global growth environment, is ill-equipped to absorb a prolonged period of $90+ crude. They point to the potential for aggressive RBI rate hikes, significant rupee depreciation, and a sharp slowdown in corporate earnings as inevitable consequences. This perspective often highlights India's structural reliance on oil imports as its Achilles' heel, making it particularly vulnerable to geopolitical energy shocks. They might highlight that while India's forex reserves are robust (over $640 billion), a sustained CAD could erode them over time, impacting external stability.
Conversely, the 'bullish' perspective emphasizes India's improved macroeconomic resilience compared to previous oil shocks. Proponents argue that India's domestic demand remains robust, government capex is strong, and a diversified economy can better absorb external shocks. They might also point to the government's strategic oil reserves and its diplomatic efforts to secure diversified energy supplies. Furthermore, some bulls might contend that the current oil spike is primarily a 'risk premium' that could dissipate quickly if geopolitical tensions de-escalate, preventing a long-term inflationary spiral. They might also suggest that the Indian market has shown resilience in past crises, and the current run-up in equities reflects a deeper structural growth story that can withstand temporary headwinds.
Actionable Investor Playbook: Navigating the $90 Oil Environment
Given the significant market implications, investors need a well-defined strategy:
- Buy/Accumulate: Consider increasing exposure to upstream oil and gas companies like ONGC and Oil India. These are direct beneficiaries of higher crude prices. Defence stocks like HAL and BDL also offer a thematic hedge against geopolitical uncertainty. Look for companies with strong balance sheets and consistent dividend payouts to weather volatility.
- Sell/Reduce Exposure: Prune holdings in highly fuel-sensitive sectors such as airlines (SpiceJet, IndiGo), and potentially logistics. OMCs (HPCL, BPCL) should be approached with caution due to potential government intervention in pricing. Consider reducing exposure to consumer discretionary stocks if inflation significantly impacts consumer spending.
- Watchlist: Monitor auto stocks (Tata Motors, Maruti Suzuki) for demand destruction signals. Keep an eye on petrochemical companies for margin erosion. For IT services, watch global client spending trends closely.
- Entry Points: For potential beneficiaries, look for dips during broader market corrections caused by negative sentiment. For vulnerable sectors, consider booking profits on any rallies.
- Time Horizon: This is likely a medium-term theme (6-18 months) until geopolitical stability returns or alternative energy sources gain significant traction. Short-term traders will find high volatility, while long-term investors should assess the fundamental shift in energy costs.
- Hedge: Consider inverse ETFs or options strategies for highly impacted sectors if you have a strong conviction on downside.
Risk Matrix: Assessing Probabilities in a Volatile Landscape
- Further Escalation of Middle East Conflict (High Probability): The geopolitical landscape remains highly unpredictable. Any direct conflict involving major oil producers or transit routes could send crude prices soaring past $100-$110, leading to a severe global economic shock and intense market volatility.
- Aggressive RBI Monetary Tightening (Medium-High Probability): If inflation prints consistently above the RBI's target, particularly due to crude-led price increases, the central bank will likely act decisively with rate hikes, significantly impacting credit growth and economic expansion.
- Significant Rupee Depreciation (Medium Probability): A widening CAD and sustained FPI outflows, exacerbated by higher oil prices, could lead to a sharper depreciation of the INR beyond current levels, making imports even more expensive and fueling a vicious cycle.
- Global Demand Destruction (Medium Probability): Sustained high oil prices globally could trigger a broader economic slowdown, dampening demand for Indian exports and impacting corporate earnings across the board, even for sectors not directly tied to fuel costs.
What to Watch Next: Catalysts and Data Points
Investors must closely monitor several key data points and events:
- Geopolitical Developments in the Middle East: Any de-escalation or further intensification of conflict will be the primary driver of crude prices. Pay attention to diplomatic efforts, military movements, and statements from key regional and global powers.
- OPEC+ Meetings and Production Decisions: Upcoming OPEC+ meetings will be crucial. Any changes in production quotas or rhetoric from major producers will directly impact supply expectations.
- RBI Monetary Policy Reviews (Next: Early June 2024): The RBI's stance on interest rates, inflation projections, and growth outlook will provide critical insights into India's economic management. Any hawkish surprises could trigger market corrections.
- India's Inflation Data (CPI & WPI, Monthly): Consistent monitoring of Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Wholesale Price Index (WPI) data will indicate the extent to which crude price increases are translating into broader inflationary pressures.
- India's Trade Deficit and Current Account Data (Quarterly): These figures will reveal the impact of higher oil imports on India's external balance. A rapidly widening CAD will signal vulnerability.
- Global Economic Indicators: Data from the US, Eurozone, and China (e.g., manufacturing PMIs, retail sales, GDP growth) will indicate the health of the global economy, which indirectly influences oil demand and risk appetite.
The current surge in Brent crude above $90 is not a fleeting event but a structural challenge demanding a strategic response from investors. Understanding the nuanced impact on India's economy and specific sectors is paramount to navigating the volatility and positioning portfolios for resilience and potential growth in this new energy paradigm.

title: HDFC Bank vs SBI: The king is still standing. But the challenger is closing in

content:
State Bank of India, the largest bank, declared its results on Friday, and investors were keen to analyse the various operational parameters of the bank, in a bid to understand the local impact of the Middle East crisis.
Let’s dig in to find out how SBI performed on various parameters and compare its performance to its nearest rival, HDFC Bank, the largest private sector bank.
Q1FY27 Credit Surge: How SBI’s 18.9% Loan Growth Outpaced HDFC
Now, let’s analyse SBI’s core operational performance and how it compares with HDFC Bank.
SBI has the largest branch network of more than 23,000 branches pan India, and it helped the bank to give a strong challenge to the ‘nimbler and growth oriented’ HDFC Bank.

SBI grew its advances by 18.9% y-o-y to Rs 49.9 lakh crore, and to the largest bank’s credit, it had grown its SME loans by 22.3% y-o-y while agri loans grew 25.4%. Retail loans also grew 15.2% y-o-y.
Credit growth is an operational parameter of a bank that is keenly tracked.
Core operational performance of SBI v/s HDFC Bank in the June 2026 quarter
| Bank | Growth in lending (% change y-o-y) | Growth in deposits (% change y-o-y) | Net Interest Margin (%) | 
| SBI | 18.9% | 9.7% | 3% | 
| HDFC Bank | 15.6% | 14.9% | 3.4% (on interest earning assets) | 
Smaller rival, HDFC Bank grew its advances by nearly 15.6% y-o-y to Rs 30.37 lakh crore, and the bank has highlighted loans to small and mid-market enterprises grew by 18.7% y-o-y in the quarter under review.
The June quarter is typically a ‘slack’ season for credit, with individuals, small and large companies still evaluating their financial objectives for the new financial year. Also, it is a quarter where a large number of families are on holiday and demand for credit is typically slack. It is commendable that both banks grew their loans by double digits in the quarter.
Of equal importance, SBI’s deposits grew 9.7% y-o-y to Rs 60.05 lakh crore with the bank reporting growth of 9.9% in time deposits, largely fixed deposits. And savings bank deposits grew 10.3% y-o-y.
Deposits form the basis of extending credit for a bank, short and long-term to clients.
Meanwhile, HDFC Bank grew its deposits by 14.9% y-o-y to Rs 31.67 lakh crore and that was led by a 17.4% y-o-y rise in term deposits (mainly fixed deposits) to Rs 21.45 lakh crore.
The Margin Battle: Why HDFC Bank Defends a 3.40% NIM
Net Interest Margin (NIM) is another key operational metric tracked by investors. For SBI, in its key domestic operations, it was 3% and broadly similar to a year earlier.
Earlier, HDFC Bank highlighted its NIM was 3.40% based on interest earning assets as compared to 3.5% a year earlier.
The RBI left the repo rate unchanged in its monetary policy meeting on Wednesday, and it has broadly signaled a continuation of its policy of lower interest rates in the economy and boosting overall lending in the banking system. This has created temporary pressure on NIMs of banks, like HDFC Bank, and banks have for several quarters focused on higher margin loans like gold, vehicle and SME loans.

SBI’s asset quality has continued to remain strong, and virtually matching HDFC Bank, which has one of the lowest NPA ratios in the domestic banking industry and is often viewed as the benchmark.
SBI’s % of net NPAs was 0.38% as compared to 0.47% a year earlier. SBI has highlighted its lowest NPA ratio in more than two decades.

Lower provisioning helped SBI offset the near 9% y-o-y fall in other income to Rs 15,922 crore. SBI has highlighted a 31.7% y-o-y decline to Rs 4,319 crore in its profit on sale / revaluation of investments. The above decline could be partly attributed to rising 10-year government bond yields, given the Gulf War and rising interest rates globally. Rising government bond yields result in losses for banks, like SBI.
Nevertheless, strong loan growth helped SBI’s standalone net profit rise by 10.2% y-o-y to Rs 21,121 crore.
For HDFC Bank, its % of net NPAs to net advances was 0.41% as compared to 0.47% a year earlier.
Its provisions were Rs 3,059.7 crore as compared to Rs 14,441 crore a year earlier, since HDFC Bank had made a floating provision of Rs 9,000 crore for FY26. HDFC Bank had made a gain of Rs 9,128 crore in the June 2025 quarter from the offer for sale related to IPO of HDB Financial Services.
HDFC Bank’s tax expenses jumped 93% y-o-y to Rs 6,048 crore in the June 2026 quarter, and as a result, its standalone net profit rose just 5 % y-o-y to Rs 19,059 crore in the quarter under review.

SBI’s Disappointing FY27 Loan Growth Forecast Weighs on Sentiment as HDFC Tackles Governance
Investors will continue to watch the local impact of the Middle East crisis on SBI and HDFC Bank, amongst other banks, in terms of rise in NPAs, NIMs and any signs in slowdown in credit growth, going forward.
However, the Reserve Bank of India on Wednesday raised its real GDP growth forecast for FY27 to 6.7% from 6.6%, while keeping the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%.
For SBI, investors will be keenly watching if the bank can sustain its loan growth momentum over the next few quarters. The top management in the press conference has highlighted credit growth target of 14%-15% y-o-y during FY27, and that is broadly lower than what has been achieved in Q1FY27.
In addition, volatility in government bond yields and its financial impact on SBI and other banks will be closely tracked by investors, going forward.
Meanwhile, HDFC Bank has tried to address corporate governance concerns with the recent appointment of Rajiv Kumar as part-time chairman of the bank, and he has also got RBI approval.
However, a cause for concern for investors is that in late July 2026, with regard to Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation (MSRDC) and garnering deposits in 2017 and 2021, the HDFC Board had decided to issue warning letters and monetary penalty of ₹1 lakh for three senior employees (the Managing Director & CEO, Chief Financial Officer and Group Head – Retail Assets), and warning letters for the remaining employees.
Investors will continue to keep a close eye on corporate governance at HDFC Bank, going forward.

title: HDFC Bank vs SBI: One bank wins on RoA, the other on credit momentum—Which fits your 2026 watchlist?
snippet: May 9, 2026 · SBI has attempted to match the operational performance of the ‘nimbler and result-oriented’ HDFC Bank in the March 2026 quarter, in terms of loan and deposit growth.
content:
State Bank of India (SBI) India, the largest bank in the country, reported its results on Friday. Investors were keen to analyse the performance of this key bank on various operational parameters.
Let’s dig in to find out how SBI performed on various parameters and compare its performance to its nearest rival, HDFC Bank, the largest private sector bank.
March 2026 quarter – SBI’s core operations give strong competition to HDFC Bank
Now, let’s analyse the March 2026 results of SBI and how do they compare with HDFC Bank.
Core operational performance of SBI v/s HDFC Bank
| Bank name | Growth in lending (% change y-o-y) | Growth in deposits (% change y-o-y) | Net Interest Margin (%) | 
| SBI | 17.2% | 11% | 2.93% | 
| HDFC Bank | 12.1% | 14.4% | 3.53% (on interest earning assets) | 
SBI has the largest branch network of23,265branches at the end of Q4FY26 pan India, and it helped the bank to give a strong challenge to the ‘nimbler and growth oriented’ HDFC Bank.
SBI grew its advances by 17.2% y-o-y to Rs 48.77 lakh crore in the March 2026 quarter. To the largest bank’s credit, it had grown its SME loans by 21% y-o-y in Q4FY26 while agri loans grew 19.7%.
The March quarter is typically a ‘busy’ season for credit, with individuals, small and large companies borrowing funds heavily before the close of the financial year.
Credit growth is an operational parameter of a bank that is keenly tracked.
Smaller rival, HDFC Bank, recorded credit growth of 12.1% y-o-y to Rs 29.37 lakh crore in the March 2026 quarter. The largest private sector bank saw strong demand from small and mid-market loans that grew by 17.2% y-o-y and business banking that grew by 20% y-o-y in the fourth quarter of FY26.
Of equal importance, SBI’s deposits grew 11% y-o-y to Rs 59.75 lakh crore in Q4FY26, with the bank reporting strong growth in time deposits, largely fixed deposits.
Deposits form the basis of extending credit for a bank, short and long-term to clients.
Meanwhile, HDFC Bank’s deposits grew 14.4% y-o-y to Rs 31.05 lakh crore in Q4FY26, and that was also owing to strong growth in time deposits.
Managing NIM pressure – strong growth in high-margin loans to SME
Net Interest Margin (NIM) is another key operational metric tracked by investors.For SBI, in its key domestic operations, it was 2.93% in the March 2026 quarter as against 3.14% a year earlier.
Earlier, HDFC Bank, highlighted it’s NIM was 3.53% on interest earning assets in the March 2026 quarter as against 3.7% a year earlier.
Loans for retail and SMEs enable banks to earn a higher rate of interest on loans / credit as against loans to top-rated corporates, and help them manage the pressure on NIMs.
The RBI has taken several steps to boost lending in the broader banking system and this includes the cut in repo rates in early December 2025. This in turn has put a temporary pressure on NIMs of banks, like SBI and HDFC Bank.
29% decline in other income for SBI
SBI’s other income dropped to Rs 17,314.1 crore in the March 2026 quarter from Rs 24,366.7 crore a year earlier.
The largest bank in its results presentation highlighted its forex / derivative income was Rs 1,258 crore in the March 2026 quarter as against Rs 2,859 crore.
Also, it incurred a loss on sale / revaluation of investments of Rs 1,471 crore in Q4FY26 as compared to a profit of Rs 6,879 crore a year earlier.
The above loss could be partly attributed to rising 10-year government bond yields, given the Gulf War and rising interest rates globally. Rising government bond yields result in losses for banks, like SBI.
Asset quality remains strong for both banks
SBI’s asset quality has continued to remain strong in Q4FY26, and virtually matching HDFC Bank, which has one of the lowest NPA ratios in the domestic banking industry and is often viewed as the benchmark.
SBI’s % of net NPAs was 0.39% in the March 2026 quarter as compared to 0.47% a year earlier.
SBI’s provisions for non-performing assets were Rs 3,140.5 crore in the March 2026 quarter as against Rs 3,964.2 crore a year earlier. The largest bank in the country has highlighted that its provision coverage ratio was 74.4 % at the end of the Q4FY26, broadly in tune with a year earlier.
SBI’s provisioning is well above regulatory requirements.
A sharp decline in other income of SBI resulted in its standalone net profit rising by just 5.6% y-o-y to Rs 19,683.8 crore in Q4FY26.
For HDFC Bank too, its asset quality has also been quite stable — its % of net NPAs to net advances was 0.38% in the March 2026 quarter as against 0.43% a year earlier.
Its provisions have also come down by nearly 18% y-o-y to Rs 2,609.6 crore in the March 2026 quarter, and it helped HDFC Bank’s standalone net profit to rise 9% y-o-y to Rs 19,221 crore in the quarter under review.
SBI and HDFC Bank’s core banking operations are reflected in their respective standalone results.
Return on Assets (RoA) – HDFC Bank races ahead
SBI has highlighted its return on assets (net asset basis – annualised) was 1.07% in Q4FY26, and it was 1.12% for FY26.
Smaller rival, HDFC Bank’s return on assets (average) – not annualized was 0.48% in the March 2026 quarter, and for FY26 it was 1.94%.
HDFC Bank along with smaller rival, Kotak Mahindra Bank, have one of the highest Return on Assets (ROA) in the banking industry, over the past several quarters.
Growth opportunities and investor concerns
SBI plans to raise $2 billion (nearly Rs 18,000 crore) from international markets, and this comes at a time when the central government has been urging industries across sectors including cement, steel, auto and engineering, amongst others, to expand their capacities. The SBI board will meet on May 12 to finalise the details of the above fund raising plan.
Investors on Dalal Street will continue to monitor SBI, HDFC Bank and other leading banks on key operational parameters, going forward – deposit and loan growth, NIM and level of NPAs. The RBI over the past several quarters has taken steps to boost lending in the broader banking system.
Investors are also awaiting a long-term truce in the Middle East war, and the current crisis has led to shortage of various petroleum products in the country.
Various domestic and international bodies have lowered the growth forecast for the Indian economy to 6% to 6.5% for FY27, given the Middle East war.
Also, the impact of the Middle East war on the local economy will be closely tracked by investors, and whether there is a rise in NPAs in the broader banking system.
SBI v/s HDFC Bank – which bank offers reasonable valuations
Now, let’s take a look at the valuations of SBI and compare it to that of HDFC Bank.
SBI v/s HDFC Bank valuations

| HDFC Bank | 2.2 times |
