title: Google Cloud vs AWS: 103% Growth Outpaces Azure [2026]
snippet: Nov 6, 2026 · Alphabet reported Google Cloud revenue of $30.7B for Q3 2026, up 103% year over year, and attributed the growth primarily to enterprise AI infrastructure, AI solutions, core Google Cloud Platform services, and TPU demand.
content:
Google’s cloud unit just posted its best growth stretch since the pandemic-era cloud boom, and it caught much of Wall Street off guard. Alphabet reported on April 29, 2026 that Google Cloud revenue jumped 63% year over year to $20.03 billion in the first quarter, and the pace didn’t let up from there: by the second quarter of 2026, Google Cloud revenue climbed to $24.8 billion, up 82% year over year, according to Alphabet, and on October 28, 2026 Alphabet reported that Google Cloud revenue grew 103% year over year in Q3 2026 to $30.7B, which means the 63% first-quarter pace has since been surpassed. That pace beat both Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure on a percentage basis (Azure grew 48% and AWS 39% in the quarter reported in October 2026), a rare result for a division that spent nearly two decades running third in the cloud market.
The number matters because Google Cloud has never led this race. AWS still commands the largest share of global cloud infrastructure spending, and Azure holds a comfortable second place. Growth rate and market share tell different stories, though, and this quarter the gap between them got a lot more interesting. Here’s what happened in the numbers, why it happened, and what a Google Cloud vs AWS growth race actually means for the rest of 2026.
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Google Cloud’s Q1 2026 Numbers, Broken Down
Alphabet filed its first-quarter 2026 results after the market closed on April 29, and the standout line wasn’t Search or YouTube. It was cloud. Google Cloud, the segment that bundles Google Cloud Platform and Google Workspace, posted $20.03 billion in quarterly revenue. That’s up from $12.26 billion in the same quarter a year earlier, a jump of 63%, and it beat what most analysts had penciled in going into the print.
Profitability climbed even faster than revenue. Google Cloud’s operating income hit $6.6 billion for the quarter, pushing its operating margin to 32.9%, up sharply from 17.8% in the year-ago period. A division that was still proving it could turn a real profit a few years back is now one of Alphabet’s more efficient businesses by margin.
The cloud strength lifted results across the whole company. Alphabet’s total revenue reached $109.9 billion, up 22% year over year, and net income more than doubled from the prior-year quarter. Yahoo Finance and CNBC both flagged cloud as the main driver behind the beat.
“Google Cloud, which includes infrastructure and corporate productivity apps, saw revenue shoot up 63% to $20.03 billion.”
CNBC, Google, Microsoft and Amazon all report cloud beats in earnings
How Google Cloud Stacks Up Against AWS and Azure
Growth rate is only half the picture, so here’s the direct comparison people are searching for. Google Cloud grew 63% year over year in Q1 2026. Microsoft Azure grew 40%. Amazon Web Services grew 28%. In a straight Google Cloud vs AWS growth comparison, Google won by 35 percentage points, even though it remains the smallest of the three by revenue. The gap held into Q2 2026, when Amazon reported AWS revenue of $42.2 billion, up 37% year over year, while Alphabet’s Google Cloud revenue reached $24.8 billion, up 82%, meaning Google’s growth rate still ran more than double AWS’s on a percentage basis even as AWS kept the far larger dollar base. The Q3 2026 results widened the pattern: AWS sales reached $46B compared with Google Cloud’s $30.7B, while Google Cloud revenue increased 103% versus AWS growth of 39%.
“Google was the standout, reporting 63% expansion, though it remains the smallest of the three.”
CNBC, Google, Microsoft and Amazon all report cloud beats in earnings
That single line captures the tension running through this earnings season. Google Cloud is growing faster than its two bigger rivals, but AWS and Azure aren’t standing still. A 28% growth rate from AWS looks modest next to 63%, except AWS is growing off a far larger revenue base: its Q1 cloud revenue was $37.6 billion versus Google Cloud’s $20.03 billion, according to Quantumrun, so the actual dollar amount it added this quarter likely still exceeds what Google added in raw terms. Azure’s 40% growth, meanwhile, keeps Microsoft comfortably ahead of Google on both share and pace.
Why Percentage Growth and Market Share Tell Different Stories
A cloud provider can grow the fastest and still be the smallest, and that’s exactly Google’s position right now. Percentage growth measures momentum. Market share measures scale. Google Cloud has plenty of the first and not much of the second, at least for now. That combination is usually what makes a market worth watching, since fast growth from a smaller player tends to force reactions from whoever is leading.
How Growth and Revenue Compare Across the Three Clouds
Alphabet reported Google Cloud revenue of $30.7B for Q3 2026, up 103% year over year, and attributed the growth primarily to enterprise AI infrastructure, AI solutions, core Google Cloud Platform services, and TPU demand. In the quarter reported in October 2026, Google Cloud led on growth with 103%, compared with Azure’s 48% and AWS’s 39%. Amazon put AWS sales at $46B for the quarter, up 39% year over year, so AWS kept the larger revenue base even as Google Cloud outpaced it on growth. CRN reported the same gap in annual run-rate terms in November 2026, with AWS at $184B in Q3 2026 versus Google Cloud’s $123B.
Synergy Research Group’s Q3 2026 figures show the same split between momentum and scale. Google Cloud’s market share rose to 16%, from 13% in Q3 2025, while AWS’s share fell to 26%, from 29% a year earlier. For readers comparing providers, the practical reading is that Google Cloud is gaining ground quickly but still sits behind AWS on both revenue and share, so a growth headline alone doesn’t settle which cloud suits a given workload.
Google Cloud also announced a partnership on October 27, 2026 to bring Google TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and on October 20, 2026 Gemini for government services entered preview as an industry-focused suite for public-sector workflows, including document redaction and constituent-data processing. Google also made Gemini 3.5 Flash generally available in air-gapped Distributed Cloud environments in October 2026, which extends its model lineup into sovereign and public-sector deployments. On the Q3 2026 earnings call, Sundar Pichai said Alphabet revenues grew 25% year-over-year and that the company is now at a half-trillion-dollar annual run rate. Buyers weighing a Google Cloud quote can treat these moves as signs that its AI infrastructure and tooling are reaching more places where enterprises already buy.
Cloud Market Share in Q1 2026: AWS Still Leads
Growth rates don’t rewrite market share overnight, and Synergy Research Group’s Q1 2026 breakdown, reported by CRN, shows exactly why. AWS held 28% of global cloud infrastructure spending in the quarter. Microsoft Azure held 21%. Google Cloud held 14%. Combined, the three companies control 63% of the market, leaving the rest split among Oracle, IBM, Alibaba, and a long tail of smaller regional providers. The next quarter pointed the same direction: per CRN, AWS held 28% of global infrastructure share in Q2 2026 while Google Cloud held 15%, and AWS’s share fell from 30% in Q2 2025 to 28%. Synergy’s Q3 2026 data continued the shift, with Google Cloud’s share rising to 16% from 13% in Q3 2025 and AWS’s share falling to 26% from 29% a year earlier.
Fourteen percent, a figure that rose to 15% in Q2 2026 and 16% in Q3 2026, looks unremarkable next to a 63% growth headline, but the trend line matters more than any single snapshot. If Google keeps growing two to three times faster than AWS, the share gap narrows gradually, not overnight. Cloud contracts run for years, and enterprise buyers rarely switch providers because of one strong quarter from a challenger.
| Cloud Provider | Parent Company | Q1 2026 YoY Revenue Growth | Q1 2026 Market Share | Operating Margin | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google Cloud | Alphabet | 63% | 14% | 32.9% | 
| Microsoft Azure | Microsoft | 40% | 21% | Not disclosed separately | 
| Amazon Web Services | Amazon | 28% | 28% | Not disclosed separately | 
| Big Three combined | n/a | n/a | 63% | n/a | 
| All other providers | n/a | n/a | 37% | n/a | 
What’s Fueling the Acceleration: AI Workloads and Custom Silicon
The obvious driver is AI demand, and Google has a structural advantage that’s easy to undersell: it designs its own AI chips. Google’s Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs, give the company a custom silicon option that doesn’t depend entirely on Nvidia GPU allocations, which have been the bottleneck for plenty of AWS and Azure customers trying to scale AI workloads fast. On November 9, 2026, Google announced TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, described as its newest TPUs for agentic workloads.
That advantage shows up directly in Google’s enterprise numbers. Paid Gemini Enterprise customers grew 40% in the quarter, and revenue from enterprise AI solutions climbed 800% year over year, though Alphabet didn’t break out the dollar base that percentage grew from. Both figures point to the same trend: companies that need AI infrastructure fast are increasingly willing to try Google Cloud instead of waiting for GPU capacity elsewhere.
Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak flagged this dynamic after the earnings call, writing that Google’s TPU and cloud business isn’t yet fully priced into Alphabet’s stock and could become a significant driver of results into 2027. That’s one analyst’s read, not a guarantee, but it lines up with how fast AI infrastructure spending is moving across the industry. Enterprise security teams evaluating new cloud AI deployments are also paying closer attention to who owns the underlying infrastructure stack, part of why Google’s $32 billion acquisition of Wiz earlier in 2026 drew so much attention at the time.
The $462 Billion Backlog
Revenue growth tells you what already happened. Backlog tells you what’s coming next. Google Cloud’s remaining performance obligations, meaning contracted revenue not yet recognized, hit $462 billion in Q1 2026, which Yahoo Finance described as nearly doubling year over year.
“Google Cloud revenue grew by 63%, driven by strong demand for AI solutions and infrastructure, with the backlog nearly doubling to $462 billion.”
Yahoo Finance, Alphabet Inc. (GOOG) Q1 2026 earnings coverage
On the earnings call, Google executives said just over 50% of that backlog is expected to convert to recognized revenue within 24 months. That’s an unusually long runway for a cloud business, and it suggests the current growth rate isn’t a one-quarter fluke tied to a handful of splashy AI deals. Multi-year contracts with AI labs and large enterprises take time to sign and even longer to fully draw down, so a backlog this size gives Google Cloud a level of revenue visibility that both AWS and Azure would likely also welcome, though neither company published a directly comparable figure this reporting cycle.
Alphabet’s Capex Bet: $190 Billion and Rising
None of this growth comes free. Alphabet spent $35.7 billion in capital expenditures in the first quarter of 2026 alone, with roughly 60% of that going toward servers. For the full year, the company raised its 2026 capex guidance to a range of $180 billion to $190 billion, a massive bet on data centers, custom chips, and AI infrastructure.
That kind of spending only makes sense if demand keeps showing up in revenue, and so far it has. But Google Cloud’s margin story and its capex story are pulling in opposite directions at the same time. Operating margin is climbing, now at 32.9%, while capital spending climbs right alongside it. Alphabet is betting AI infrastructure demand stays durable enough to make both numbers work together, and the backlog figure is the clearest evidence that bet is paying off for now.
Amazon and Microsoft face the same math. Both companies run their own capex plans tied to AI infrastructure, and Alphabet’s guidance increase puts pressure on both rivals to at least match the pace, since customers evaluating cloud providers increasingly ask about GPU and TPU availability before they ask about price.
Wall Street’s Reaction: GOOGL Stock and Analyst Notes
Investors liked what they saw. Alphabet’s stock, ticker GOOGL, surged roughly 6% in after-hours trading following the April 29 report and opened at a fresh record the next trading day. That’s a large one-day move for a company of Alphabet’s size, where a 6% swing represents tens of billions of dollars in market value.
The analyst reaction reinforced the stock move. Morgan Stanley’s Brian Nowak argued the cloud and TPU business remains underappreciated by the market, a view that implies more upside if Google Cloud keeps this growth pace through the rest of 2026. Whether that view holds depends heavily on whether the current AI infrastructure boom continues at its current intensity, which is far from guaranteed given how fast capital spending and compute demand can shift in this industry.
Sundar Pichai and How Google Is Framing the Quarter
Google’s own executives were eager to take a victory lap on the earnings call. Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai highlighted the cloud results directly, and his framing tells you what the company wants investors to focus on.
“The Google Cloud segment delivered outstanding results in the first quarter. Cloud revenues accelerate across all key areas and were up 63% to $20 billion.”
Sundar Pichai, CEO, Alphabet and Google, Q1 2026 earnings call transcript
Pichai’s framing puts the growth rate front and center rather than dwelling on market share, and that makes sense from Google’s side of the table. A company sitting in third place has every incentive to talk about direction rather than current standing. It’s a fair point, since the direction increasingly favors Google, but it’s also a framing choice a distant leader like AWS wouldn’t need to make.
A Brief History of the Cloud Wars
Context helps explain why 63% growth is such a big deal. Amazon launched AWS in March 2006, effectively creating the modern public cloud market from scratch. For most of the two decades since, AWS has been the runaway leader, with Microsoft building Azure into a strong second place and Google Cloud consistently running third, often by a wide margin.
Google Cloud has had fast growth quarters before. Alphabet reported 46% year-over-year cloud growth in both Q4 2020 and Q1 2021, during the pandemic-driven rush to move workloads online. Those were considered standout quarters at the time. The 63% figure from Q1 2026 cleared that bar by 17 percentage points, and it has since been topped by the 103% year-over-year growth Alphabet reported on October 28, 2026 for Q3 2026, which makes Q3 Google’s strongest cloud growth quarter in the period covered by available reporting.
The revenue trajectory tells the same story from a different angle. Google Cloud didn’t cross $10 billion in quarterly revenue until Q4 2024, when it posted $11.955 billion, up from $9.57 billion the prior quarter. About five quarters later, quarterly revenue reached $20.03 billion, and by the second quarter of 2026 it had climbed again to $24.8 billion, up 82% year over year according to Alphabet, before reaching $30.7B in Q3 2026. Nearly doubling a cloud business this size in about a year and a half is rare, and it’s the clearest sign yet that Google’s AI infrastructure bet is turning into paying customers, not just headlines.
| Period | Metric | Value | 
|---|---|---|
| Q4 2020 | Google Cloud YoY revenue growth | 46% | 
| Q1 2021 | Google Cloud YoY revenue growth | 46% | 
| Q3 2024 | Google Cloud quarterly revenue | $9.57 billion | 
| Q4 2024 | Google Cloud quarterly revenue | $11.955 billion (first quarter above $10B) | 
| Q1 2025 | Google Cloud quarterly revenue | $12.26 billion | 
| Q1 2026 | Google Cloud quarterly revenue | $20.03 billion | 
| Q1 2026 | Google Cloud YoY revenue growth | 63% | 
Why 63% Is a Bigger Deal Than It Sounds
Growth rates get harder to sustain as the revenue base gets larger, which is standard math for any company. Google Cloud grew 46% off a much smaller base back in 2020 and 2021. Producing 63% growth off a base roughly double the size of its 2020 revenue is a tougher trick, and it’s the main reason analysts like Nowak are paying closer attention now than they did during the earlier growth spurt.
How AWS and Azure Are Likely to Respond
Neither AWS nor Azure is going to cede ground quietly, and both companies have their own levers to pull. AWS has leaned into its own custom AI chips, called Trainium, as a lower-cost alternative to Nvidia GPUs for training and inference, mirroring the same silicon strategy that’s helping Google right now. Expect AWS to keep pushing Trainium adoption and possibly adjust pricing on AI compute to defend its share, which Synergy Research Group put at 26% in Q3 2026.
Azure’s advantage runs through its close partnership with OpenAI, which has made Microsoft the default cloud home for a huge share of generative AI workloads built on GPT models. That relationship helped drive Azure’s 40% growth in Q1 2026, with Azure growing 48% year over year in the quarter reported in October 2026 (reportedly about $33.2 billion in revenue), and it isn’t going away. If anything, Azure’s next moves likely focus on expanding data center capacity fast enough to keep up with OpenAI’s own growth, since capacity constraints, not lack of demand, have been the more common bottleneck across the industry.
Both rivals also have far larger revenue bases than Google Cloud, which means smaller percentage moves still translate into large dollar figures. The real thing to watch isn’t one dramatic announcement from either company. It’s whether AWS and Azure’s growth rates hold steady, accelerate, or slip further behind Google’s pace over the next two or three quarters.
Market Impact: What This Means for Enterprise Cloud Buyers
For IT leaders choosing between cloud providers, this earnings cycle adds a genuine third option to serious AI infrastructure conversations that used to start and end with AWS or Azure. Google’s TPU pricing and availability, combined with Gemini Enterprise’s 40% customer growth, gives procurement teams a credible reason to at least request a Google Cloud quote alongside the usual two names.
That doesn’t mean switching costs have disappeared. Multi-cloud and single-cloud enterprises alike still face real migration costs, data gravity concerns, and staff retraining time when they add or shift providers. But the backlog data suggests large customers are already signing on, not just kicking the tires. A $462 billion backlog doesn’t build itself from small trial deployments alone.
There’s a security dimension enterprise buyers can’t ignore either. As cloud providers compete harder for AI workloads, the attack surface tied to cloud infrastructure keeps expanding too, part of why infrastructure-level threat activity and cloud security tooling choices like endpoint detection platforms remain a parallel conversation to which provider wins on price and performance.
| Metric | Q1 2026 Value | Year-over-Year Change | 
|---|---|---|
| Alphabet total revenue | $109.9 billion | +22% | 
| Google Cloud revenue | $20.03 billion | +63% | 
| Google Cloud operating income | $6.6 billion | Margin up from 17.8% to 32.9% | 
| Google Cloud backlog (RPO) | $462 billion | Nearly doubled | 
| Alphabet quarterly capex | $35.7 billion | Part of $180-190B full-year guidance | 
| Paid Gemini Enterprise customers | Not disclosed in dollars | +40% | 
| Enterprise AI solutions revenue | Not disclosed in dollars | +800% | 
What This Means for Developers and Engineering Teams
For engineers who actually build on these platforms, the headline growth numbers translate into something more concrete: capacity. Google’s TPU generations have become easier to provision for teams outside its own AI labs, and Vertex AI’s tooling has matured enough that fewer teams describe it as a distant third option behind AWS SageMaker and Azure Machine Learning. None of that shows up directly in an earnings report, but it’s the on-the-ground reality behind the Gemini Enterprise customer growth number cited above.
Multi-cloud setups remain the norm for larger engineering organizations, and nothing about this quarter changes that math. Teams running inference on TPUs while keeping storage and networking on AWS, or using Azure for identity and Google Cloud for data analytics, are common, and Google’s growth doesn’t require anyone to go all-in on a single vendor. What it does mean is that GPU shortages elsewhere make TPU access a more realistic fallback than it was even a year ago, which matters for any team that has had a training job stuck in a GPU queue for days at a time.
The pricing conversation is shifting too. As Google Cloud pushes for share, engineering leads negotiating renewal contracts with AWS or Azure now have a credible alternative to cite, even if they never plan to migrate a production workload. That leverage is worth something at renewal time, no matter which cloud a team picks in the end to run its workloads on. It also raises the stakes on portability. Teams that leaned hard into one provider’s proprietary services over the past few years may find themselves with less negotiating room than teams that kept core workloads reasonably portable.
But for the people writing the infrastructure-as-code configs and signing off on architecture decisions, this quarter is the strongest evidence yet that treating Google Cloud as an afterthought next to AWS and Azure is no longer a safe assumption.
5 Predictions for Google Cloud Through 2027
Where does this go from here? Based on the numbers in this report, here’s a reasonable read on the next few quarters.
- Growth stays elevated. Google Cloud likely keeps outgrowing AWS and Azure through 2026.
- The backlog buys time. With roughly half of the $462 billion backlog set to convert within 24 months, Google Cloud has revenue visibility that should support strong growth into 2027 even if new bookings cool off.
- AWS pushes Trainium harder. Expect Amazon to promote its custom AI chips more aggressively and possibly adjust AI compute pricing to protect its share, which fell to 26% in Q3 2026, from further erosion.
- Capex guidance climbs industry-wide. Alphabet’s move to $180-190 billion in 2026 capex pressures Amazon and Microsoft to match or exceed their own spending plans, keeping the data center buildout race intact into 2027.
- Market share still moves slowly. Even with Google Cloud’s growth advantage, expect it to remain in third place by share through the end of 2026. Gains from a 14% base take years of sustained outperformance, not one strong quarter.
The takeaway: Google Cloud had its best quarter in years, and the numbers back up the story Google wants to tell. AWS and Azure aren’t losing yet, not by share, but the growth math is no longer tilted entirely in their favor the way it was even two years ago.
Frequently Asked Questions
Why did Google Cloud grow 63% in Q1 2026?
Growth was driven mainly by AI infrastructure demand, including custom TPU chips and Gemini Enterprise adoption, which grew 40% in paid customers during the quarter. Revenue from enterprise AI solutions climbed 800% year over year.
Is Google Cloud bigger than AWS now?
No. Google Cloud held about 14% of the global cloud infrastructure market in Q1 2026, compared to AWS’s 28% and Microsoft Azure’s 21%, according to Synergy Research Group data reported by CRN. In the Google Cloud vs AWS comparison, Google is growing faster but remains the smallest of the three by both revenue and market share.
What is Google Cloud’s operating margin?
Google Cloud’s operating margin reached 32.9% in Q1 2026, up from 17.8% in the same quarter a year earlier.
What does Google Cloud’s $462 billion backlog mean?
Backlog, or remaining performance obligations, is contracted revenue that hasn’t been recognized yet. Google’s backlog nearly doubled year over year to $462 billion, and executives said just over half of it should convert to revenue within 24 months.
How much is Alphabet spending on AI infrastructure in 2026?
Alphabet raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to a range of $180 billion to $190 billion, after spending $35.7 billion in the first quarter alone, with about 60% going toward servers.
Did AWS and Azure also grow in Q1 2026?
Yes. AWS grew 28% year over year and Microsoft Azure grew 40% year over year in the same period, and both remain ahead of Google Cloud in total market share.
How did Alphabet’s stock react to the earnings report?
Alphabet shares surged roughly 6% in after-hours trading following the April 29, 2026 report and opened at a fresh record the next session.
Will Google Cloud overtake Azure in market share?
Not in the near term based on current data. Google Cloud would need several more years of growth well above Azure’s pace to close the gap between Azure’s 20% and Google’s 15% share of cloud infrastructure in Q2 2026, since market share shifts far more slowly than quarterly growth rates.

title: Google Cloud Grew 82% vs AWS 37%: What It Means
snippet: Jul 23, 2026 · Google Cloud’s revenue jumped 82% year-over-year to $24.8 billion in the quarter ended June 2026, accelerating from 63% growth on $20.0 billion the quarter before. Alphabet reported the number on July 22 in its second-quarter shareholder message. One week later, on July 30, Amazon reported AWS sales of $42.2 billion, up 37% year over year. AWS is still the larger business, but Google Cloud ...
content:
Google Cloud’s revenue jumped 82% year-over-year to $24.8 billion in the quarter ended June 2026, accelerating from 63% growth on $20.0 billion the quarter before. Alphabet reported the number on July 22 in its second-quarter shareholder message. One week later, on July 30, Amazon reported AWS sales of $42.2 billion, up 37% year over year. AWS is still the larger business, but Google Cloud is growing more than twice as fast. Alphabet scheduled its third-quarter 2026 report for October 28, 2026 and Amazon for October 29, 2026; this article covers the June quarter.
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.
How big was Google Cloud’s 82% quarter?
Alphabet’s second-quarter 2026 results, released July 22, showed Google Cloud revenue of $24.8 billion, up 82% and accelerating from the prior quarter’s 63%, a gain of 19 percentage points in one quarter.
“Cloud revenue grew 82%, powered by strong demand for AI infrastructure and AI solutions,” said Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet and Google, in the company’s second-quarter shareholder message. The quarter also marked Alphabet’s twelfth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth.
Two details make this more than a typical beat. The growth rate accelerated rather than leveling off, which is unusual for a business of this size. And it came while Google Cloud’s operating margin expanded: operating income reached $8.8 billion on a 35.6% margin, a sign the growth was not simply bought with discounts.
The backlog and the first-quarter baseline
The June quarter builds on a record first quarter. Alphabet’s first-quarter 2026 results filed with the SEC showed consolidated revenue of $109.9 billion, up 22%, with Google Cloud contributing $20.0 billion on 63% growth. Cloud’s operating margin expanded to 32.9% in that quarter, up from 17.8% a year earlier, and its sales backlog nearly doubled sequentially to $462 billion.
The backlog (remaining performance obligations in Alphabet’s filings) kept climbing in the June quarter to $514 billion, up from $106 billion a year earlier, with just over half expected to convert into recognized revenue within the next 24 months. A growing backlog means customers are signing multi-year cloud and AI infrastructure contracts faster than Google can recognize the revenue. In the first quarter, Google Cloud accounted for roughly 18% of Alphabet’s total revenue ($20.0 billion of $109.9 billion).
A backlog is a signed commitment, not recognized revenue, so the useful test is conversion. If revenue growth stays high while the 24-month conversion window runs, the backlog is doing its job. If the backlog keeps growing but revenue growth fades, customers may be committing faster than Google can deliver capacity. Our calculation: the backlog rose $52 billion from the March quarter ($514 billion minus $462 billion) and is about 4.85 times its year-earlier level ($514 billion divided by $106 billion). Half of $514 billion is about $257 billion, or roughly $32 billion a quarter over eight quarters if conversion were even, against $24.8 billion of revenue in the June quarter.
Profit and contract volume against revenue
Lined up side by side, the last two quarters show profitability and contract volume rising along with the top line.
| Metric | Q1 2026 (quarter ended March) | Q2 2026 (quarter ended June) | 
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $20.0 billion | $24.8 billion | 
| Year-over-year growth | 63% | 82% | 
| Operating margin | 32.9% | 35.6% | 
| Operating income | About $6.6 billion (derived: 32.9% of $20.0 billion) | $8.8 billion | 
| Backlog | $462 billion | $514 billion | 
Google Cloud grew faster, converted more of that growth into profit, and signed bigger multi-year contracts in the June quarter than in the March quarter. Revenue rose $4.8 billion (24%) from the March quarter, and operating income rose about $2.2 billion, so the incremental margin was about 46%. The backlog is the figure to watch most closely.
How do Azure and AWS compare with Google Cloud’s pace?
Azure’s steady 40%
Where Google Cloud swung from 63% to 82% in a single quarter, Azure has held steady. In the quarter ended September 2025, Microsoft reported that Azure and other cloud services revenue grew 40%, or 39% in constant currency, while the broader Intelligent Cloud segment brought in $30.9 billion, up 28%. Microsoft Cloud overall, which bundles Azure with Microsoft 365 commercial cloud and other services, hit $49.1 billion, up 26%.
In the quarter ended March 2026, the latest Azure quarter covered here, Azure grew 40% again, matching the company’s own forecast almost exactly. Total Microsoft revenue for that quarter was $82.9 billion, up 18%, with net income of $31.8 billion. Copilot’s paid user base climbed 33% since January to 20 million seats, a second growth engine layered on top of Azure infrastructure demand.
Two quarters at almost exactly 40% suggest a growth rate Microsoft can sustain rather than one lifted by a single large contract. That predictability is what enterprise buyers and investors tend to reward.
AWS’s 37% quarter
Amazon is the incumbent, and its latest quarter showed AWS sales of $42.2 billion, up 37% year over year. Amazon reported its second-quarter 2026 results on July 30, after the market closed, calling the 37% its fastest AWS growth in 18 quarters, at a $169 billion annualized revenue run rate.
The March quarter set up that jump. AWS segment revenue reached $37.6 billion, up 28% year-over-year, which Amazon executives called the fastest growth in 15 quarters.
Google Cloud and AWS before the third-quarter reports
Alphabet was scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 results on October 28, 2026, and Amazon on October 29, 2026. The latest figures covered here are Google Cloud at $24.8 billion, up 82%, and AWS at $42.2 billion, up 37%. The 82% belongs to the June quarter, not the third quarter.
The 82% versus 37% comparison measures year-over-year quarterly growth, not market share. AWS still posts the larger quarterly revenue figure, so any claim that Google Cloud has overtaken AWS is wrong.
Backing out the year-ago bases (revenue divided by one plus the growth rate) gives roughly $13.6 billion for Google Cloud and $30.8 billion for AWS. That means Google Cloud added about $11.2 billion of revenue year over year and AWS about $11.4 billion, nearly the same in dollars, and Google Cloud’s revenue moved from about 44% of AWS’s to about 59%. These are derived, rounded figures, and each company defines its cloud segment its own way, so treat the dollar comparison as approximate.
For buyers, the practical rule is to hold off on changing multi-year commitments until you have read how each company describes cloud growth and capital spending in the third-quarter reports.
Growth rates side by side
| Company | Prior Quarter Growth | Latest Quarter Growth | Trend | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Google Cloud | 63% (quarter ended March 2026) | 82% (quarter ended June 2026) | Accelerating | 
| Microsoft Azure | 40% (quarter ended September 2025) | 40% (quarter ended March 2026) | Steady | 
| AWS | 28% (quarter ended March 2026, fastest in 15 quarters) | 37% (quarter ended June 2026) | Accelerating | 
AWS is not struggling. A 37% growth rate on a business that posted $42.2 billion in a single quarter is large in absolute terms, and few companies of that size grow that fast for long. The story is that Azure and Google Cloud are growing faster off smaller bases, and Google Cloud is now outgrowing both of its bigger rivals.
Who leads cloud market share?
AWS still leads. According to Synergy Research Group’s cloud infrastructure market-share report for the first quarter of 2026, AWS held 28% of the global cloud infrastructure services market, Microsoft Azure held 21%, and Google Cloud held 14%. Together the three hyperscalers captured 63% of the market.
The market is enormous and still expanding. Enterprise spending on cloud infrastructure services reached $129 billion in the first quarter of 2026, pushing the annualized run rate past $500 billion for the first time.
| Provider | Global Cloud Infrastructure Market Share (Q1 2026) | Most Recent Reported Growth Rate | Latest Reported Cloud Revenue | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon Web Services | 28% | 37% year-over-year (quarter ended June 2026) | $42.2 billion | 
| Microsoft Azure | 21% | 40% year-over-year (quarter ended March 2026) | Not disclosed separately* | 
| Google Cloud | 14% | 82% year-over-year (quarter ended June 2026) | $24.8 billion | 
| All other providers combined | 37% | Varies by provider | Varies by provider | 
*Microsoft reports Azure inside a combined Intelligent Cloud segment that also includes enterprise services. That segment posted $30.9 billion in revenue for the quarter ended September 2025.
This is why the market share conversation cannot stop at a single ranking. AWS leads by a wide margin in dollars and share, but a smaller base compounds faster in percentage terms. In the June quarter AWS added only slightly more dollars year over year than Google Cloud, so the share gap is under pressure if those growth rates persist.
The takeaway for a buyer is that share moves slowly while growth rates move fast. One point of share in a market this size is a lot of revenue, but the ranking will not flip on a single quarter. Judge a vendor on the trend across several quarters, not on one headline growth number.
How much are the hyperscalers spending on AI?
All three are spending heavily on data centers, custom silicon, and power capacity. CNBC’s live coverage of the July 22 earnings call put Alphabet’s 2026 capital-expenditure forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion and Amazon’s 2026 investment budget at approximately $220 billion. The company documents are Alphabet’s second-quarter shareholder message and Amazon’s second-quarter 2026 release. Our Microsoft, Meta and Google AI capex analysis covers the wider spending picture.
Cloud revenue is accelerating, and capital spending is accelerating right alongside it. That is why Google Cloud’s margin stood out: 17.8% a year earlier, 32.9% in the March quarter, 35.6% in the June quarter. Growing fast while spending heavily is normal. Doing both while expanding margin is not.
How do the three AI bets differ?
AWS leans on Anthropic and custom silicon
Amazon is pairing its Anthropic partnership with its own Trainium chips, betting that custom silicon plus a deep partnership with a leading model developer will keep enterprise customers inside the AWS ecosystem.
Azure leans on OpenAI and Copilot
Microsoft’s early OpenAI partnership gave Azure first-mover status in enterprise generative AI, and Copilot’s climb to 20 million paid seats gives Microsoft a software layer that pulls more Azure consumption behind it.
Google Cloud leans on Gemini and TPUs
Google Cloud sells its own Gemini models plus custom TPU infrastructure directly to enterprise customers, an approach now showing up in its accelerating growth and its $514 billion backlog. After the first-quarter results, Fortune reported, “Google Cloud now represents 18% of the company’s overall business.”
What are Wall Street and enterprise buyers watching?
Strong growth does not automatically lift the stock. When Alphabet reported first-quarter results in April, Google Cloud grew 63%, yet shares slipped in after-hours trading as investors focused on the scale of planned capital spending. Investors may weigh capex against the growth headline again in the third-quarter reports.
For enterprise buyers, the practical concern is cost. Heavier AI infrastructure investment across all three hyperscalers may filter down into pricing, data transfer fees, and contract terms over time.
What should enterprise IT and FinOps teams do with this?
Faster hyperscaler growth generally means more aggressive sales pushes, more bundled AI services turned on by default, and more complexity in tracking which workloads deliver value. That is part of why FinOps has moved from a niche discipline to a standard line item on enterprise IT budgets.
Multi-cloud, once viewed mainly as a risk hedge, is increasingly used as a bargaining tool, since a credible threat to shift workloads carries more weight when the rival is posting 82% growth. A workable rule: use a faster-growing vendor’s appetite for share to win better terms, but keep contract lengths short enough that you can react if the third-quarter reports change the picture. For price differences on GPU capacity, see our AWS vs Azure vs Google Cloud GPU pricing comparison.

title: The $700B AI Infrastructure Race: Who Wins in 2026?
snippet: Mar 30, 2026 · Big Tech is spending $700B on AI infrastructure in 2026. Here is what Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are building and whether it will pay off.
content:
The $700B AI Infrastructure Race: Who Wins in 2026?
Big Tech is spending $700B on AI infrastructure in 2026. Here is what Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are building and whether it will pay off.
Table of contents
TL;DR
Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are collectively planning to spend approximately $690 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, with the vast majority directed at AI data centers, GPUs, and networking equipment. This is up sharply from the approximately $405 billion these companies spent in 2025.1 Amazon leads with a projected $200 billion, followed by Alphabet at $175–185 billion, Microsoft at $120 billion or more, Meta at $115–135 billion, and Oracle at $50 billion. The bet is that AI-powered cloud services will generate trillions in revenue over the next decade — but right now, AI services generate only a fraction of what is being spent, and several of these companies face negative free cash flow as a result.
What You'll Learn
In this article, you will learn the specific dollar amounts each hyperscaler is committing to AI infrastructure in 2026, what they are building with that money, the business rationale behind each company's bet, the growing gap between infrastructure spending and AI revenue, and what this all means for the broader technology industry.
Why $700 Billion? The Forces Driving the Spend
The spending surge is driven by a single reality: demand for AI compute is outstripping supply across every major cloud provider. Inference workloads — running trained AI models to serve predictions, generate text, and produce images — now account for an estimated 60 to 70 percent of total AI compute demand across major hyperscalers, up from roughly 40 percent in 2024.2 As enterprises adopt AI agents, copilots, and multimodal applications, the compute requirements are scaling faster than anyone anticipated.
Every major cloud provider reported in their most recent earnings calls that they are "capacity-constrained" — they have more customer demand than they can serve. This is the core justification for the spending: it is not speculative building, but building to meet contractual backlogs worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
The Spending Breakdown: Company by Company
Amazon: $200 Billion
Amazon's 2026 capital expenditure plan of $200 billion is the largest of any hyperscaler and represents a roughly 50 percent increase over its 2025 spend of approximately $131 billion.3 The majority of this investment flows into AWS data centers — specialized facilities increasingly designed for the liquid cooling and massive power requirements of trillion-parameter large language models. AWS has also launched "AI Factories," a new offering that deploys dedicated AI infrastructure for enterprise and government customers.3
The business case: AWS reported a contractual backlog of $244 billion, meaning customers have already committed to spending that much on AWS services in the coming years.4 Key investments include an $11 billion AI campus in Indiana and a $12 billion facility in Louisiana.
The market reaction was harsh. The $200 billion figure exceeded analyst expectations by roughly $50 billion, and combined with a below-expectation profit outlook, Amazon shares fell more than 10 percent in after-hours trading.5 Morgan Stanley analysts project Amazon could face negative free cash flow of approximately $17 billion in 2026, while Bank of America estimates the deficit at $28 billion.6
Alphabet: $175–185 Billion
Alphabet announced 2026 capital expenditure guidance of $175 billion to $185 billion, which at the top end would be more than double its 2025 capex spend.7 Roughly 60 percent of the investment goes to servers and 40 percent to data centers and networking equipment.
The spending is split between Google DeepMind's AI research compute and Google Cloud's customer-facing AI services. Google Cloud's backlog surged 55 percent sequentially and more than doubled year-over-year, reaching $240 billion at the end of Q4 2025.8
CEO Sundar Pichai acknowledged the scale of the investment, and Fortune characterized his comments as signaling that even this level of spending "still won't be enough" to meet demand.9 Despite beating earnings expectations, Alphabet shares dipped in extended trading, reflecting Wall Street's nervousness about the sheer magnitude of the spending.
Microsoft: $120 Billion and Rising
Microsoft's fiscal year 2026 capital expenditure is projected at approximately $120 billion, though some analyst estimates run as high as $146 billion — a more than 230 percent increase from just two years ago.10 In Q2 fiscal 2026 alone, Microsoft reported a record $37.5 billion in capital expenditures, adding nearly 1 gigawatt of data center capacity — equivalent to the power consumption of a mid-sized city.11
Microsoft faces a unique constraint: despite a total demand backlog that has more than doubled to $625 billion, CFO Amy Hood has said the company remains "capacity-constrained" due to power limitations, not lack of customer demand.12 The company is investing heavily in custom "Maia" AI chips to reduce dependence on Nvidia GPUs and improve margins.
Microsoft stock has taken the hardest hit among the hyperscalers, trading near $374 as of late March 2026 with a year-to-date decline of approximately 21 percent.13
Meta: $115–135 Billion
Meta's AI capital expenditure projection of $115 billion to $135 billion is nearly double its 2025 outlay.14 The company has also announced plans to invest $600 billion in data centers by 2028.15 Unlike the other hyperscalers, Meta's infrastructure investment is primarily for its own AI products — powering recommendation systems, content moderation, generative AI features across Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp — rather than for selling cloud services to external customers.
To offset these costs, Meta is reportedly planning layoffs that could affect up to 20 percent of its workforce, roughly 16,000 of its approximately 79,000 employees.16 A Meta spokesperson called the reports "speculative." The company has already reduced its Reality Labs workforce by 1,500 positions earlier in 2026, reallocating resources from metaverse projects to AI research and development.17
Oracle: $50 Billion
Oracle's fiscal year 2026 capex is expected to reach approximately $50 billion, a 136 percent increase over 2025.18 Oracle is financing this through a combination of $25 billion in debt and an equivalent amount raised through secondary share offerings and convertible stock.19
The customer list driving Oracle's AI data center demand reads like a directory of the AI industry: Nvidia, Meta, OpenAI, AMD, TikTok, and xAI are all Oracle Cloud Infrastructure customers.20 Oracle reported $523 billion in remaining performance obligations, signaling strong contracted demand.21
The Revenue Gap: Will the Bet Pay Off?
The central question facing the industry is whether the revenue will ever match the investment. The numbers are sobering.
According to Menlo Ventures, companies spent approximately $37 billion on generative AI in 2025, up from $11.5 billion in 2024 — a 3.2x year-over-year increase.22 That is still a small fraction of the more than $400 billion hyperscalers spent on infrastructure that same year. Only about 25 percent of enterprise AI initiatives have delivered their expected return on investment to date, and fewer than 20 percent have been scaled across entire enterprises.23
The five largest hyperscalers' combined debt is projected to climb from $356 billion to $433 billion in 2025, even as their operating cash flow rises from $378 billion to $577 billion over the same period — Bank of America notes this actually makes their debt-to-cash ratio lighter, from 0.94 to 0.75, leaving room for further borrowing.24 This represents a fundamental shift from the historically cash-funded business models of Big Tech.
The bull case is straightforward: AI is a platform shift comparable to cloud computing itself, and the companies that control the infrastructure will capture the majority of value created. AWS took over a decade from its 2006 launch to become consistently profitable. The AI infrastructure build-out is following a similar trajectory, just at a much larger scale.
The bear case is equally straightforward: the ratio of spending to revenue is unprecedented, and if enterprise AI adoption stalls or open-source models reduce the premium customers are willing to pay for cloud AI, these investments could take far longer to recoup than planned. As the recent shutdown of OpenAI's Sora demonstrated, even the most impressive AI products can fail spectacularly when the economics do not work.
What This Means for Developers and the Tech Industry
For developers and technology professionals, this infrastructure build-out has several practical implications.
First, AI-related cloud services are getting cheaper, fast. The competition among hyperscalers is driving down prices for inference, training, and GPU rentals. Google's Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, released in March 2026, is priced at just $0.25 per million input tokens, reflecting the push toward affordable AI compute.25 If you are building AI-powered applications, the cost of compute is falling in your favor.
Second, the job market is shifting. Meta's potential layoffs of 16,000 employees is part of a broader trend: tech layoffs in 2026 have surged to at least 59,000 across the industry, with Amazon, Meta, and Block among the largest cutters.26 The spending is creating demand for infrastructure engineers, ML operations specialists, and data center technicians, while reducing demand for roles that AI can partially automate.
Third, the GPU cloud comparison is more relevant than ever. With every hyperscaler capacity-constrained, developers building AI products need to understand the pricing, availability, and performance trade-offs across providers. The best GPU deal today may not be the best deal in six months as new capacity comes online.

Frequently Asked Questions
How much are hyperscalers spending on AI in 2026?
The five largest hyperscalers — Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle — are collectively planning approximately $690 billion in capital expenditures for 2026, with the vast majority directed at AI infrastructure including data centers, GPUs, and networking equipment.
Which company is spending the most on AI infrastructure?
Amazon leads with a projected $200 billion in 2026 capital expenditures, most of which funds AWS data centers. Alphabet follows at $175–185 billion, Microsoft at $120 billion or more, Meta at $115–135 billion, and Oracle at approximately $50 billion.
Is AI infrastructure spending profitable?
Not yet at the current scale. Companies spent approximately $37 billion on generative AI in 2025 according to Menlo Ventures, a fraction of the more than $400 billion hyperscalers spent on infrastructure that year. The companies are betting on long-term returns as enterprise AI adoption accelerates.
Why is Meta laying off employees while spending $135 billion on AI?
Meta's planned layoffs of up to 20 percent of its workforce are intended to offset the cost of AI infrastructure investment. Unlike other hyperscalers, Meta does not sell cloud services to external customers, so its AI spending must be justified by improvements to its own products and advertising business.
What does this mean for cloud computing prices?
Competition among hyperscalers is driving AI compute prices down. Inference costs have fallen significantly in 2026, and new efficiency-focused models like Google's Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite are priced as low as $0.25 per million input tokens.

title: Amazon vs. Alphabet: Which AI Cloud Stock Makes the Better Case After the Spending Bill?
snippet: Oct 4, 2026 · Amazon's cloud business earns almost twice as much operating profit as Google Cloud. Google Cloud is growing more than twice as fast. Choosing between the stocks requires deciding which...
content:
Amazon's cloud business earns almost twice as much operating profit as Google Cloud. Google Cloud is growing more than twice as fast. Choosing between the stocks requires deciding which advantage will survive the enormous bill for building the next generation of AI infrastructure.
Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) give shareholders much more than cloud exposure. Retail and advertising are critical at Amazon; Search and YouTube are at Alphabet. The cloud businesses can change the growth trajectory, but shareholders own the full companies, including their spending obligations. A low headline P/E is particularly unhelpful when investment gains inflate both companies' reported net income.
For illustration purposes only. Photo by Brett Sayles on Pexels
Amazon has the larger profit engine
Amazon's July 30 report showed AWS generated $42.2 billion of June-quarter revenue and $16.6 billion of operating income, a 39.4% margin. Revenue increased 37% from a year earlier. That is substantial growth for a business already producing more than $50 billion of trailing annual operating profit.
Alphabet reported on July 22 that Google Cloud's revenue rose 82% to $24.8 billion, with $8.8 billion of operating income and an approximately 35.6% margin. Its smaller base leaves more room for rapid expansion, although investors should resist projecting one exceptional growth rate indefinitely.
These margins are useful, but they are not identical measures of fully burdened shareholder returns. Alphabet records substantial shared AI research costs outside its Cloud segment. Neither segment's operating margin deducts the entire current cash cost of new infrastructure. Depreciation spreads equipment costs over time, while shareholders fund capacity before its revenue is fully established.
Alphabet offers a lower operating-profit hurdle
At the October 2 close, Alphabet traded at approximately 27.8 times trailing operating income on an enterprise-value basis, compared with 30.3 times for Amazon. Both figures value the consolidated company. They should not be mistaken for standalone cloud multiples. Alphabet's figure includes around $19 billion of preferred equity added to the standard enterprise value.
Both feature in our 10 Stocks With New Strategic Partnerships Investors Should Watch. Several companies on that list collect fees from financing or implementing AI instead of owning the cloud platforms. Those alternatives carry different claims on the same spending cycle.
The discount favors Alphabet, but cash conversion stops this from being an easy bargain claim. Its trailing free cash flow was $53.3 billion, while its latest quarter consumed $5.9 billion after property and equipment purchases. The annual figure still benefits from earlier quarters with lower investment spending.
Amazon's company-defined trailing free cash flow was negative $7.6 billion. Its calculation deducts equipment purchases net of sales proceeds and incentives, whereas Alphabet deducts property and equipment purchases. The measures are therefore not perfectly identical. Even with that favorable netting, Amazon's recent investment exceeded its operating cash generation.
Alphabet also raised equity and preferred capital in June, alongside additional debt. Strong historical profits do not mean the current expansion is being financed entirely from internally generated cash. For both stocks, future utilization and the durability of margins matter more than the size of the announced spending budget.
The choice depends on what improves next
Insider Monkey's hedge fund database counted 369 Amazon holders in Q2 2026, up from 353 in Q1 2026 , and 275 Alphabet holders, up from 265. Arrowstreet increased its Amazon common-share position approximately 23.8% to 40.35 million shares. Fisher Asset Management increased its Alphabet position about 2.4% to 39.99 million shares. These filings provide historical positioning, not a forecast of cloud returns.
September 15 short interest totaled around 81.44 million Amazon shares, about 0.8% of float, and 87.39 million Alphabet Class A shares, about 1.5% of that class's float. Neither snapshot settles the capital-spending debate.
I favor Alphabet at these valuations: faster Cloud growth and a lower consolidated operating-profit multiple offer the more appealing combination. The bear case is that Search economics weaken while infrastructure spending stays elevated, reducing the cash support behind Cloud's expansion.
Amazon could overturn that preference if AWS maintains its stronger margin while retail improvements and maturing infrastructure lift cash after investment. Its risk is paying a higher operating-profit multiple before that cash recovery appears. The most useful next evidence is not another record spending announcement. It is whether each new dollar of capacity begins generating enough additional cash to make the spending easier to fund.
While we acknowledge the potential of AMZN and GOOGL as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. title: Tata Motors EV Sales Surge 90% in Q2FY27
snippet: Tata Motors EV sales rose 90% in Q2FY27 as domestic revenue hit a record, even while a JLR-led one-time loss pulled the ...
content:
Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles reported a consolidated net loss of Rs 5,531 crore for the September quarter of FY27, even as domestic passenger-vehicle revenue rose 51% and electric-vehicle volumes increased 90% year on year, highlighting the uneven financial transition accompanying India’s shift towards cleaner mobility.
Revenue from operations rose 33.9% year on year to Rs 96,920 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 72,349 crore in the same quarter a year earlier. Total expenses increased 23.3% to Rs 97,827 crore from Rs 79,310 crore. The company also recognised a one-time loss of Rs 6,738 crore during the quarter.
The consolidated performance was significantly affected by Jaguar Land Rover, Tata Motors’ British luxury vehicle subsidiary. JLR reported revenue of £5.9 billion, up 20.3% year on year, while profit before tax and exceptional items stood at £6 million, compared with a loss of £485 million in the year-ago quarter. However, it recorded exceptional items of £530 million, mainly linked to restructuring, separation costs and asset and intangible-asset write-downs.
JLR reported free cash outflow of £540 million in the quarter and closed with cash of £1.8 billion. Total liquidity stood at £6 billion as of September 30, 2026. Citing continuing market challenges, geopolitical risks and exceptional costs, the company revised its full-year FY27 guidance to an adjusted EBIT margin of 2-3% and free cash outflow of around £1.25 billion.
Tata Motors’ domestic passenger-vehicle business recorded its highest-ever quarterly revenue of Rs 20,400 crore, up 51% year on year. Vehicle volumes grew 40%, which the company said was significantly ahead of industry growth. Electric-vehicle volumes rose 90% year on year, and the business reported a 380-basis-point sequential improvement in market share.
The domestic business retained the second position in India’s passenger-vehicle market, with a Vahan market share of 14.3% in Q2FY27. Its electric-vehicle market share stood at 43%, despite increased competition and the entry of new players. Alternative powertrains accounted for more than half of the portfolio mix, including EV penetration of 23% and CNG penetration of 28%.
The stronger sales performance did not translate into higher margins. Domestic passenger-vehicle EBITDA margin fell to 4%, down 180 basis points year on year, while EBIT margin declined to negative 0.3%. Tata Motors attributed the pressure to adverse commodity prices and foreign-exchange movements. Profit before tax and exceptional items was at breakeven, compared with about Rs 200 crore in the corresponding quarter.
The domestic passenger-vehicle business generated positive free cash flow of Rs 825 crore during the quarter, taking first-half free cash flow to Rs 1,945 crore. Its closing cash balance was Rs 11,000 crore and gross debt was Rs 3,100 crore, resulting in net cash of Rs 7,900 crore.
During the quarter, Tata Motors introduced its global consumer-facing identity, TATA.CARS, launched the Tata Aeris and made product interventions across the Curvv and Sierra portfolios. It also extended its Battery-as-a-Service offering across its electric-vehicle range and signed a memorandum of understanding with Stellantis to provide access to advanced product technology and vehicle architecture for global products.
The company entered the third quarter with monthly volumes of 75,400 units in October, its highest-ever level. Shailesh Chandra, Managing Director and CEO of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, said the company recorded quarterly sales of more than 200,000 units and would focus on sustaining growth, expanding EV penetration, ramping up production capacity and improving profitability.
JLR said it plans to begin deliveries of three luxury electric vehicles—the Range Rover Electric, Range Rover Sport Electric and Jaguar Type 01—in early 2027. It also plans to introduce the Range Rover GT and an all-new electric Defender next year. The company said its Enterprise Missions programme remained on track to deliver £1.7 billion in savings over the next two years.

title: Tata Motors PV reports 34% revenue growth in Q2 FY27
snippet: Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited announced strong Q2 FY27 results with consolidated revenues up 34% YoY to ₹96.9K Cr. JLR revenue grew 20.3%, while Tata PV domestic revenue surged 51%.
content:
Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited announced its financial results for the second quarter and half-year ended September 30, 2026. The company reported a consolidated revenue of ₹96.9K Cr, a significant increase of 34% year-on-year. This growth was driven by strong momentum across both its domestic and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) businesses. The company also reported improved EBITDA margins and PBT.
Tata Motors PV Announces Strong Q2 FY27 Financials
Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited (formerly Tata Motors Limited) has announced robust financial results for the quarter and half-year ended September 30, 2026. The company showcased a commendable performance, with consolidated revenues reaching ₹96.9K Cr, marking a substantial year-on-year growth of 34%. This surge in revenue highlights the company’s sustained growth momentum across its diverse business segments.
Key Financial Highlights
Consolidated Performance
In the second quarter of FY27, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited achieved consolidated revenues of ₹96.9K Cr, up 34% YoY. The EBITDA margin stood at 6.2%, reflecting a 630 bps improvement YoY, while the EBIT margin saw a significant rise of 790 bps YoY to 1.1%. These improvements are largely attributed to the recovery from the cyber incident at JLR in the previous year. However, sequential margins were impacted by an adverse mix and persistent commodity cost pressures. Consolidated PBT (before exceptional items) was ₹0.4K Cr. The company also reported a consolidated Free Cash Flow (FCF) of (₹6.3)K Cr, resulting in a Net Debt of ₹50.8K Cr as of September 30, 2026.
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) Performance
JLR demonstrated strong performance with revenue for Q2 FY27 at £5.9bn, up 20.3% YoY. The EBITDA Margin for JLR was 6.6%, an increase of 820 bps, and the EBIT Margin improved to 1.1%, up 970 bps. The company reported profit before tax and exceptional items of £6m for Q2. JLR unveiled three new luxury electric vehicles, including the Range Rover Electric, Range Rover Sport Electric, and Jaguar Type 01, signaling a strategic push towards electrification.
Tata Passenger Vehicles (Tata PV) Performance
The domestic business recorded its highest-ever quarterly revenue at ₹20.4K Cr, a significant 51% growth YoY. However, the EBITDA margin for Tata PV was 4.0%, a decrease of 180 bps YoY, and the EBIT Margin was (0.3)%, down 50 bps YoY. Despite strong growth, margins were compressed due to adverse commodities and FX impact. PBT (before exceptional items) for Q2 FY27 was at breakeven. The company launched the new Tata Aeris and introduced multiple smart product interventions, strengthening its market position.
Looking Ahead
The company anticipates that global geopolitical volatilities, luxury segment demand trends, EV adoption pace, and commodity costs will remain key monitorables. Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited plans to continue driving industry-beating growth for its domestic business while improving margins through focused cost reductions and calibrated pricing. For JLR, the focus will be on building sales momentum from new EV launches and demonstrating progress in its Enterprise Missions plan.
Management Commentary
Shailesh Chandra, Managing Director & CEO, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited, stated, “Q2 FY27 was another quarter of strong execution for Tata Motors PV, with record quarterly sales of 200k+ units and industry-beating growth of 40% YoY reflecting robust customer demand across our portfolio. We maintained our leadership in electric mobility, recording industry-beating growth of 90% YoY in EV sales. Building on the momentum of our Q1 launches, we further strengthened our portfolio with new launchings including the all-new Tata Aeris. We also unveiled our new customer-facing identity, TATA.CARS, reflecting the evolution of our brand in step with the aspirations of today’s Indian car buyer. We registered a Y-o-Y revenue growth of 51% and our highest ever quarterly revenues of ₹20.4K Cr in Q2FY27. While steep commodity cost pressures remained a headwind, we responded through calibrated pricing and focused cost actions. Looking ahead, we remain focused on sustaining industry-beating growth, capitalizing on growing EV-penetration, ramping up production capacity and strengthening profitability.”
Source: BSE

snippet: The AI chip selloff has dragged Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO | AVGO Price Prediction) into a steep one-month decline, and the custom ...
content:
Broadcom Is Still Down 22% in the Past Month: Is AVGO Stock Really on a Road to Recovery?
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
The AI chip selloff has dragged Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO | AVGO Price Prediction) into a steep one-month decline, and the custom AI chip leader hasn’t joined the latest rebound. Broadcom stock is down 22% over the past month to $292.21 in afternoon trading. Even as most chipmakers rally back, the stock is up just 0.2%.
Politics set the background. AI and chip stocks sold off on November 4 and November 5 after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections, raising fears of tighter rules on data center construction. For Broadcom, which designs custom accelerators for a small group of hyperscalers and AI labs, the open question is whether the stock is set up for a recovery or still has more downside.
Broadcom’s Bull Case Rests on Surging AI Revenue
On September 2, Broadcom reported Q3 FY2026 revenue of $29.6 billion, up 86% year over year (YoY). AI semiconductor revenue at the company reached $16.7 billion, up 221% YoY and 54% sequentially. Looking ahead, Broadcom guided Q4 FY2026 revenue to $34.8 billion and AI semiconductor revenue to $21.7 billion, a 236% YoY jump.
Broadcom CEO Hock Tan told analysts on that call, “Q3 demand was simply hot, and we’re just getting started.” Tan also stated, “In 2027, we have secured the supply to again double AI revenue to approximately $115 billion.” Those comments framed the AI ramp at Broadcom as a multiyear story.
The valuation adds to the bull argument. At 19x forward earnings, Broadcom is valued far below Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) at 42x, a cheaper way into the same AI budgets. Addressing the political risk, Gavekal U.S. chief economist Will Denyer said, “There will always be some state and some county who is willing to welcome data centers.” That view suggests Broadcom’s customers could move projects to friendlier locations.
Broadcom’s Bear Case Centers on Political Risk and Margins
Custom AI chips from Broadcom go straight into the hyperscale data centers now facing political scrutiny, so a construction slowdown could hit its sales directly. Tan noted that dependency himself on the same call: “To deploy an AI data center at scale, land, power and shell are major constraints and dictate timing.” Those constraints sit largely outside the company’s control, and they also explain why the power, cooling, and networking suppliers behind the expansion keep getting attention of their own (we featured seven of them in a free report on the AI infrastructure trade). Broadcom also reveals that a limited number of significant customers drive its AI semiconductor business.
Analysts expect Broadcom’s earnings per share to grow 67% in fiscal 2027, compared with 110% for AMD, which helps explain the lower multiple. Management’s Q4 outlook calls for gross margin of 73%, down from 78% a year earlier, as memory-heavy custom accelerators take a larger share of Broadcom’s sales. A quiet response to the chip rebound may suggest investors want proof before stepping back in.
How NVIDIA, AMD and Marvell Stack Up Against Broadcom
NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock is down 22% over the past month to $187.43, a slide almost identical to the one at Broadcom. AMD stock is down 31% over the past month to $445.98. The steepest decline of the four has come from Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL), whose stock is down 52% over the past month to $138.53.
The business models differ more than the price charts suggest. Merchant accelerators from NVIDIA and AMD are sold to any cloud provider, backed by their own software and networking platforms. Broadcom co-designs custom accelerators with individual customers and pairs them with AI networking silicon and VMware-based infrastructure software. Marvell, a custom-chip rival, sits closest to that model by combining custom silicon with optical and switching chips.
Broadcom’s December Report Is the Next Big Test
Broadcom’s next test is whether its December earnings report delivers on its Q4 AI semiconductor guidance. The bullish case rests on triple-digit AI growth, a far lower forward multiple than AMD and customers that can shift data centers to friendlier states. On the other side sit political risk aimed directly at Broadcom’s customers, slower expected earnings growth and contracting gross margin.
Whether the past month’s slide marks a bottom or a pause for Broadcom remains an open call for each reader. A cautious approach could make sense until the debate over Broadcom’s AI guidance resolves.

title: AMD vs. Broadcom: With NVDA's Jensen Huang Gone, Which AI Stock Wins the Most?

content:
AMD vs. Broadcom: With NVDA’s Jensen Huang Gone, Which AI Stock Wins the Most?
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Which AI chip stock belongs in a retirement-focused portfolio right now—AMD (NASDAQ:AMD | AMD Price Prediction) or Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO)—with Jensen Huang out at NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA)? Huang resigned on November 12, 2026 after reports of personal misconduct and a board investigation, and CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. AMD and Broadcom stock got a boost from Nvidia’s loss, then both sold off on Friday. AMD fell 8.75% to $534.06, and Broadcom fell 4.76% to $347.01.
Each company stands to gain from NVIDIA’s problems in a different way. AMD sells Instinct GPUs that compete head-on with NVIDIA’s chips. Broadcom co-designs custom accelerators for hyperscalers and supplies the networking that connects them. The comparison below covers three areas, and if you want the longer view on what the next monster chip winner tends to look like early, we put the pattern in a free Next Nvidia playbook.
Valuation: Broadcom Is the Cheaper Way to Own AI Growth
AMD trades at a trailing P/E of 202, a forward P/E of 35 and 130.79 times free cash flow. Its free cash flow yield is 0.76%. On CNBC’s Fast Money, one guest put it bluntly: “AMD is the priciest of the three, but if you look at Broadcom and Micron, they’re still trading at a much lower multiple.” Broadcom produced $13.67 billion[1] of free cash flow in a single quarter, which gives its $1.656 trillion market cap real earnings support. Winner: Broadcom.
Income and Cash Flow: Broadcom Pays You While You Wait
For retirees, this is the clearest gap between the two. Broadcom declared a $0.65 per share[1] quarterly dividend on September 2, 2026. In fiscal Q3, free cash flow rose 94.5%[1] and was 46% of revenue. Non-GAAP EPS of $3.32[1] extended its beat run to 9 consecutive quarters.
AMD shareholders receive no dividend. Its Q3 free cash flow fell 70.9%[2] to $554 million as capex jumped 151% and inventory rose to $11.46 billion. Its balance sheet is still sound, with net cash and 28.2x interest coverage. Winner: Broadcom.
Growth Trajectory: AMD Has the Most Direct Path to NVIDIA’s Customers
If AI labs move GPU orders away from NVIDIA, AMD is the obvious place for them to go. Data Center revenue reached $8.55 billion[2], up 97%, and the segment’s operating margin expanded to 34% from 25%. Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle are already running Helios racks. AMD guided Q4 revenue to about $17 billion[2], roughly 66% growth. CEO Lisa Su said, “It is true that demand is higher than supply,”[3] and expects 2027 revenue to grow more than 80%.
Broadcom’s AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.70 billion[1], and management guided to $21.7 billion for the next quarter. That figure covers custom XPUs and networking, so it should not be compared directly with AMD’s Data Center segment. Those gains depend on just six XPU customers[4]. AMD wins this category because a reallocation of GPU orders benefits it most directly, although NVIDIA’s CUDA software remains a real barrier to switching. Winner: AMD.
Verdict: Broadcom Is the Retirement Pick, by a Narrow Margin
Broadcom wins. Customers that reduce their reliance on NVIDIA without cutting AI spending will still need custom silicon and Ethernet networking. Gartner named Broadcom a leader in custom AI silicon, and its $8.75 billion[1] quarterly infrastructure software business adds diversification that AMD lacks. The dividend, the cash flow margin, and the lower multiple all give it the edge for retirement accounts.
AMD wins for younger growth investors who can live with a 2.542 beta and a 52-week range of $188.22 to $658.52. If hyperscalers move large GPU orders away from NVIDIA, AMD will likely outperform.
Both stocks carry the same broader risk. NVIDIA helped finance many of its own customers, so a break there could slow AI spending across the industry, including at both companies. Broadcom’s dependence on a small group of hyperscaler customers is the main risk to the Broadcom case.

title: Credo Technology outpaces Broadcom in AI networking growth
snippet: Credo Technology grew fiscal 2026 revenue 206% to $1.3 billion on AI interconnect demand, outpacing Broadcom's broader ...
content:
Credo Technology outpaces Broadcom in AI networking growth
Broadcom logo (public domain) via Wikimedia Commons
The small interconnect specialist tripled revenue in fiscal 2026 while its far larger rival grows across a broader business mix
Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ: CRDO) just closed a fiscal year that most chip companies only see in investor-day slide decks. Revenue for fiscal 2026, which ended in May 2026, reached $1.3 billion, up 206% from the prior year.
Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) is still the heavyweight in AI networking. On a percentage basis, though, the specialist has been running laps around the giant’s overall business.
The numbers behind the sprint
The revenue figure was not a one-quarter fluke. Credo posted triple-digit growth rates across several consecutive quarters.
Profits grew even faster. Non-GAAP earnings per share jumped 392% to $3.46 for the fiscal year.
The engine behind all of this is a product category most people never think about: the cables and chips that connect AI hardware together. Credo’s flagship is the active electrical cable, or AEC. Think of it as a copper cable with built-in electronics that keep the signal clean as data races between servers.
Credo sells these under its HiWire brand. The company pitches them on reliability and power efficiency, two features that matter a great deal in AI training clusters.
Credo’s customer list is concentrated among the biggest buyers in tech. Four hyperscalers, the massive cloud operators that build data centers by the warehouse-full, each accounted for more than 10% of revenue in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026.
Wall Street has noticed. Credo’s stock was up approximately 74% year-to-date as of mid-June 2026, ahead of both Nvidia and Broadcom over that stretch.
The news moving money, markets, and the world—before your day starts.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
David, Goliath, and a fair fight on percentages
The comparison with Broadcom needs some nuance. Broadcom’s AI semiconductor business is growing fast too.
In one reported quarter, its AI chip revenue climbed 221% year-over-year to approximately $16.7 billion. That growth rate actually tops Credo’s annual figure. The dollar amount from a single quarter also dwarfs everything Credo booked across its entire fiscal year.
Broadcom is a sprawling company. It sells custom AI accelerators and networking chips alongside a broad lineup of other products. The fast-growing AI segment gets blended with businesses that grow at a more ordinary pace, which pulls the company-wide growth rate down.
Credo has no such ballast. Nearly everything it sells feeds directly into AI data-center connectivity, so the AI boom shows up almost undiluted in its results.
From copper to light
Credo is not betting the company on copper alone. Its roadmap now leans heavily into optics, which carry data as light rather than electrical signals.
The company has been building out optical digital signal processors, the chips that clean up and decode data moving through fiber. It is also working on silicon photonics, which puts optical components directly onto silicon chips. A product line called 1.6T ZeroFlap optics rounds out the push.
As of November 2026, Credo was still focused on ramping that optical portfolio and on industry standards work.
What this means for investors and the AI build-out
Management has guided for more than 80% revenue growth in fiscal 2027. That outlook is supported by anticipated optical revenue of more than $600 million.
Customer concentration is the other obvious pressure point. Having four hyperscalers each above the 10% mark shows that the biggest buyers trust Credo’s gear.
For Broadcom holders, the read-through is less dramatic. The company’s AI chip revenue is growing at a pace comparable to Credo’s, just on a vastly larger base and inside a more diversified business.
